note: Editorial, versioned event list for the Human History timeline. Years are astronomical integers (negative = BCE; no year zero adjustment is attempted for prehistory). datePrecision states how firm the date is; contested or approximate dates say so in the summary. `wikipedia` is the English article that anchors the event and supplies its image at build time. 464 events, deliberately balanced across regions and across the civilizations in the filter list.

events.title: Sahelanthropus, an early hominin, lives in Chad
events.summary: A skull nicknamed Toumaï, found in the Djurab Desert of Chad in 2001, belongs to Sahelanthropus tchadensis and is dated to roughly seven million years ago, close to the time the human and chimpanzee lineages separated. Whether it walked upright, and whether it sits on the human side of that split at all, is actively debated among palaeoanthropologists. It is placed here as the earliest candidate ancestor, not as a settled fact, and the date carries an uncertainty of hundreds of thousands of years.

events.title: Australopithecus afarensis walks upright
events.summary: The partial skeleton known as Lucy, found at Hadar in Ethiopia in 1974, and the fossil footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania show that Australopithecus afarensis walked habitually on two legs about 3.2 to 3.7 million years ago, while still having a small, ape-sized brain. Bipedalism therefore came long before large brains in human evolution. The species persisted for nearly a million years across East Africa and is a plausible, though not certain, ancestor of the genus Homo.

events.title: The first stone tools
events.summary: Deliberately flaked stone tools from Gona in Ethiopia are about 2.6 million years old, and cruder flaked stones from Lomekwi in Kenya may be 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo itself. The Oldowan toolkit of choppers and sharp flakes let hominins butcher carcasses and crack bones for marrow, opening a richer diet. Which species made the earliest tools is unresolved; what is clear is that tool-making predates and probably helped drive the growth of the human brain.

events.title: Homo erectus spreads across Africa and Asia
events.summary: Homo erectus appears in Africa about 1.9 million years ago and, within a few hundred thousand years, is found at Dmanisi in Georgia, in Java and in northern China, making it the first hominin known to leave Africa. Taller and longer-legged than earlier species, it made the symmetrical Acheulean hand axe and probably used fire. Populations in Indonesia survived until perhaps 100,000 years ago. Its dates and the boundaries between it and related species remain matters of specialist debate.

events.title: Habitual use of fire by early humans
events.summary: Hearths at sites such as Qesem Cave in Israel and Beeches Pit in England show hominins using fire habitually by about 400,000 years ago; claims for earlier, opportunistic use at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa reach back a million years and remain debated. Cooking made more calories available from the same food and may have shaped the evolution of the human gut and brain. Fire also extended the day, warmed cold climates, and gave people a place to gather.

events.title: Neanderthals inhabit Europe and western Asia
events.summary: Neanderthals, a sister species to Homo sapiens, lived from at least 400,000 years ago until about 40,000 years ago across Europe and into Central Asia. They made complex tools, controlled fire, buried some of their dead and cared for injured members of their groups. They interbred with modern humans, and people outside Africa still carry about two percent Neanderthal ancestry. Why they disappeared is unsettled; competition, climate swings and small population size are all proposed.

events.title: Homo sapiens emerges in Africa
events.summary: The earliest fossils widely accepted as Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to roughly 300,000 years ago, with later finds at Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia. The date is a genuine estimate: it depends on thermoluminescence dating of burnt flints and on where researchers draw the line between archaic and modern anatomy. What is not contested is the geography. Every line of fossil and genetic evidence places the origin of our species in Africa, from which all later dispersals began.

events.title: Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave
events.summary: At Blombos Cave on South Africa's southern coast, people engraved cross-hatched patterns on pieces of red ochre and strung shell beads around 75,000 years ago, and mixed ochre paint in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago. These are among the oldest known signs of symbolic thought and decoration, well before the famous cave art of Europe. They show that behaviour we call fully modern arose in Africa, in step with the anatomy, rather than in a later European burst.

events.title: Modern humans spread out of Africa
events.summary: Genetic evidence points to a major dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa between roughly 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, from which most non-African populations descend, though earlier and smaller excursions into the Levant and perhaps beyond are attested by fossils. Along the way these people met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans. By around 50,000 years ago they had reached Australia, a crossing that required open-water voyaging and is among the earliest evidence of seafaring.

events.title: People reach Australia by sea
events.summary: Humans reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and finds at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land are argued to push the date to 65,000 years, a claim still debated. Getting there required crossing open sea between the islands of Wallacea, the earliest known deliberate ocean voyages. The descendants of those settlers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, maintain the longest continuous cultural traditions on Earth, recorded in rock art, song and land management.

events.title: The oldest known figurative cave art, Sulawesi
events.summary: A life-sized painting of a warty pig in the cave of Leang Tedongnge on Sulawesi, Indonesia, has been dated by uranium-series analysis of overlying mineral crusts to at least 45,500 years ago, and a hunting scene in nearby Leang Bulu' Sipong to about 44,000 years. These predate the celebrated paintings of Chauvet and Lascaux in France and show that figurative art existed in island Southeast Asia as early as anywhere. The dates are minimums; the paintings could be older.

events.title: People enter the Americas
events.summary: Humans moved from Siberia into the Americas across or along the coast of Beringia during the last glacial period. Sites such as Monte Verde in Chile, about 14,500 years old, show that people were far south before the ice-free corridor opened, and footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to around 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, a claim still being tested. The route, timing and number of migrations remain among the liveliest questions in archaeology.

events.title: Early pottery in East Asia and the Jōmon
events.summary: The world's oldest known pottery comes from Xianrendong Cave in China, about 20,000 years old, and from Japan, where the Jōmon culture was making cord-marked vessels by about 14,000 BCE, thousands of years before farming reached the archipelago. Pots allowed foods to be boiled and stored, changing diets and settlement. The Jōmon people remained largely hunter-gatherer-fishers for ten millennia, and their elaborate later vessels and clay figurines are among the earliest sustained ceramic art traditions.

events.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
events.summary: In the hills of the Fertile Crescent people began cultivating wheat, barley, lentils and peas and herding sheep and goats around 9500 BCE. Farming arose independently several times elsewhere, including rice in the Yangtze valley, maize in Mesoamerica, and millet, squash and potatoes in other regions, so no single origin is meant here. Agriculture allowed permanent villages and larger populations, but early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than the foragers they replaced.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe, monumental building before farming
events.summary: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised circles of carved limestone pillars, some over five metres tall and weighing ten tonnes, beginning around 9500 BCE, before pottery, metal or, on most readings, agriculture. The site overturned the assumption that monumental architecture and organised religion followed farming rather than preceding it. Its purpose is debated; interpretations range from a ritual centre for scattered bands to a settlement whose domestic areas are only now being excavated.

events.title: Maize is domesticated in Mesoamerica
events.summary: In the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico, people transformed teosinte, a grass with a few hard kernels, into maize around 9,000 years ago, one of the most dramatic domestications in agriculture. Maize spread north and south through the Americas, supporting the Olmec, Maya, Aztec and Inca civilisations and, after 1492, feeding much of Africa, Europe and Asia. Its nixtamalisation with lime, a Mesoamerican invention, made its niacin available and prevented pellagra.

events.title: Rice is domesticated in the Yangtze valley
events.summary: Farmers in the lower Yangtze valley of China were cultivating rice by around 7000 BCE, and genetic evidence suggests domesticated Oryza sativa japonica arose from wild rice there, with indica rice developing later in South Asia through crossing. Rice became the staple of more people than any other crop and the basis of the dense, irrigated societies of East and Southeast Asia. The dates come from charred grains and phytoliths and are approximate to a millennium.

events.title: The wheel and the wheeled vehicle
events.summary: Potter's wheels were in use in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE, and the earliest evidence for wheeled vehicles appears almost simultaneously in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and central Europe, including a pictograph from Uruk, wagon models and the Bronocice pot from Poland. Where the vehicle wheel was first invented is unknown. Drawn by oxen and later horses, carts and chariots transformed farming, trade and war, though the Americas, lacking draught animals, did without them until 1492.

events.title: Uruk becomes the world's first great city
events.summary: On the Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, Uruk grows to perhaps forty thousand people — the largest settlement on Earth — with monumental temples, mass-produced pottery, cylinder seals and the administrative recording that will shortly become writing. The 'Uruk phenomenon' spreads its styles across the Near East, and later tradition makes the city the home of Gilgamesh, hero of the world's oldest surviving epic.

events.title: Bronze metallurgy spreads
events.summary: Alloying copper with tin to make bronze, harder and easier to cast than either, was practised in Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau by about 3300 BCE, and later independently in China, where the Shang dynasty cast ritual vessels of unmatched complexity. Because tin was scarce, bronze drove long-distance trade networks from Cornwall and Afghanistan to the Aegean. Bronze weapons and tools defined an age that ended, in the eastern Mediterranean, in a wave of collapses around 1200 BCE.

events.title: Writing is invented in Mesopotamia
events.summary: Clay tablets from Uruk in southern Mesopotamia record goods and rations in a proto-cuneiform script from about 3200 BCE, the earliest writing system that can be read. Egyptian hieroglyphs appear at nearly the same time, and writing was invented again, independently, in China and in Mesoamerica. Writing began as bookkeeping and only later carried literature, law and history. Because it allows knowledge to outlive its authors, it is the conventional boundary between prehistory and history.

events.title: Narmer unifies Upper and Lower Egypt
events.summary: Around 3100 BCE the king remembered as Narmer — perhaps the Menes of later tradition — brings Upper and Lower Egypt under one crown, an act commemorated on the Narmer Palette from Hierakonpolis. The unification creates the world's first large territorial state and begins the sequence of dynasties that Egyptian priests themselves would still be counting three thousand years later. The double crown of the Two Lands remains the defining symbol of pharaonic kingship throughout.

events.title: The Austronesian expansion settles the Pacific
events.summary: Beginning from Taiwan around 3000 BCE, Austronesian-speaking voyagers spread through the Philippines and Indonesia, west to Madagascar, and east across the open Pacific, reaching Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa New Zealand by about 1250 CE. Navigating by stars, swells and birds in double-hulled canoes, they accomplish the most far-flung expansion of any people before modern times — one language family spanning half the globe.

events.title: Imhotep raises the Step Pyramid at Saqqara
events.summary: For King Djoser his chancellor Imhotep stacked six shrinking stone platforms over a burial shaft at Saqqara, turning the low mudbrick mastaba into a sixty-metre staircase to the sky. It is the earliest large building in the world made entirely of dressed stone, and it set the pyramid age going a century before Giza. Imhotep, remembered afterwards as an architect, physician and finally a god, is one of the first individuals in history known by name for what he made.

events.title: Caral and the first cities of the Americas
events.summary: At Caral in the Supe valley of Peru, monumental platform mounds, sunken plazas and residential districts were built from about 2600 BCE, contemporary with the pyramids of Egypt and older than any other urban centre in the Americas. The Norte Chico or Caral-Supe culture grew cotton for fishing nets and traded with the coast; it left no pottery and no evidence of warfare. Knotted-cord quipu found there hint at a recording system millennia before the Inca.

events.title: Cities of the Indus Valley civilisation
events.summary: Between about 2600 and 1900 BCE cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, in present-day Pakistan and northwest India, housed tens of thousands of people on planned grids with baked-brick houses, covered drains, public baths and standardised weights. Its script, on thousands of seals, remains undeciphered, so its rulers, gods and language are unknown. The civilisation declined as rivers shifted and monsoons weakened; its people did not vanish but dispersed into smaller settlements.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza is built
events.summary: Built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE, the Great Pyramid stood as the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly four thousand years. Its roughly 2.3 million blocks were quarried, moved and set with copper tools, ramps, levers and a large, organised, paid workforce housed in a nearby town, not by enslaved labour as once assumed. The precision of its alignment to the cardinal points shows Old Kingdom Egypt commanded advanced surveying and administration.

events.title: Stonehenge's sarsen circle is raised
events.summary: The great sarsen stones of Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in England, were raised around 2500 BCE within an earlier earthwork begun about 3000 BCE; the smaller bluestones were hauled from the Preseli hills of Wales, 250 kilometres away. The monument is aligned on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, and burials show it was a place of the dead. Its builders left no writing, so its exact meaning is unknown, but it is the best-studied of Europe's Neolithic megaliths.

events.title: Sargon of Akkad builds the first empire
events.summary: Sargon, a cupbearer turned king, conquers the Sumerian city-states and rules from the Persian Gulf toward the Mediterranean — the first time many peoples and languages are held under one government. His dynasty standardises administration in Akkadian, garrisons distant provinces, and becomes the model of universal kingship that Mesopotamian rulers invoke for two thousand years. His daughter Enheduanna is the first author in history known by name.

events.title: Enheduanna, the first author known by name
events.summary: Sargon of Akkad installed his daughter as high priestess of the moon god at Ur, and she signed her work. The hymns attributed to Enheduanna, above all the Exaltation of Inanna, speak in the first person about exile and restoration, and they were copied in Babylonian scribal schools for centuries afterwards. She is the earliest writer in any language whose name is attached to surviving compositions. Some Assyriologists argue the attribution is a later tradition rather than contemporary authorship, and the debate is unsettled.

events.title: The Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest surviving law code
events.summary: Three centuries before Hammurabi, the Sumerian kings of Ur issued a set of rulings in the form later codes would follow: a prologue claiming the king had protected the orphan and the widow, then case-by-case law. Its penalties are strikingly monetary — a fixed weight of silver for an injury where Babylon would later demand an eye. It survives on broken clay copies, so perhaps forty of its clauses can be read. Whether Ur-Nammu or his son Shulgi issued it is disputed.

events.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh is composed
events.summary: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, circulate by around 2100 BCE and are later woven into a Babylonian epic — the oldest long literary work that survives. Its hero befriends the wild man Enkidu, grieves his death, and travels to the world's edge seeking immortality, meeting a survivor of a great flood along the way. Lost for two millennia, the epic was recovered from Nineveh's library and deciphered in 1872, stunning readers with a flood story older than Genesis.

events.title: Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt and opens the Middle Kingdom
events.summary: After roughly a century in which the Old Kingdom's central state had broken into rival provincial houses, the Theban king Mentuhotep II defeated the northern dynasty at Herakleopolis and ruled a single Egypt again. His terraced funerary temple at Deir el-Bahari, built into the cliffs opposite Thebes, announced a new style later copied by Hatshepsut next door. The Middle Kingdom he began is the period Egyptians themselves treated as their classical age of literature and language. The dates are reconstructed and carry a margin of decades.

events.title: The outrigger and the sailing canoe open the ocean
events.summary: Austronesian boatbuilders solved the problem that limits any narrow hull — it capsizes — by lashing a float on a spar to one or both sides, and added a fore-and-aft crab-claw sail that lets a canoe work to windward. Planks were sewn or lashed to the hull rather than nailed, giving a flexible boat that could be repaired at sea. The combination carried people and their pigs, taro and breadfruit across half the planet, and the double-hulled version is the ancestor of the modern catamaran.

events.title: The Code of Hammurabi
events.summary: Hammurabi, king of Babylon, had nearly three hundred legal rulings carved on a basalt stele around 1755 BCE, covering contracts, wages, property, family and injury. It is not the oldest law code, but it is the longest and best preserved from the ancient Near East, and it is publicly displayed law, meant to be seen. Its principle that the strong should not oppress the weak, stated in the prologue, sits beside penalties that varied sharply by social class.

events.title: The Lapita people settle the western Pacific
events.summary: Between about 1500 and 900 BCE seafarers making distinctive dentate-stamped pottery spread from the Bismarck Archipelago east through the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, the first people to reach these islands. Their ancestry combined Austronesian speakers from Taiwan and island Southeast Asia with Papuan populations. Carrying pigs, dogs, chickens, taro and yams in outrigger canoes, the Lapita are the ancestors of the Polynesians, whose later voyages settled the remote Pacific.

events.title: The Vedas are composed
events.summary: The Rigveda, a collection of over a thousand hymns in an early form of Sanskrit, was composed in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent between about 1500 and 1200 BCE and transmitted orally with extraordinary precision for many centuries before being written down. The later Vedas, Brahmanas and Upanishads, composed down to about 500 BCE, developed ritual, philosophy and the ideas of karma and rebirth. They form the oldest scriptural layer of Hinduism, the world's third-largest religion.

events.title: Tyrian purple, the dye that named a people
events.summary: Along the Lebanese coast, workshops crushed murex sea snails by the tens of thousands, fermented the glands and produced a dye that deepened rather than faded in sunlight. It took perhaps ten thousand shells for a few grams, which made purple cloth worth its weight in silver and eventually restricted by Roman law to emperors. The Greek name for the dye, phoinix, is probably the root of the word Phoenician. Mounds of discarded shells still mark the old dyeing sites at Tyre and Sidon.

events.title: Egypt's New Kingdom empire at its height
events.summary: From Thutmose III's campaigns to the long reign of Ramesses II, New Kingdom Egypt rules from Nubia to Syria — the largest empire Egypt ever holds. Karnak and Luxor swell with temple building, Tutankhamun's brief reign leaves the tomb that will astonish the modern world, and the battle of Kadesh against the Hittites ends in history's first surviving international peace treaty.

events.title: Hatshepsut rules as king and sends a fleet to Punt
events.summary: Regent for her stepson, Hatshepsut took the full titles of a king and held them for two decades, one of very few women to rule Egypt in her own right. Her reign was a building and trading boom rather than a war: obelisks at Karnak, the colonnaded terraces of Deir el-Bahari, and a seaborne expedition to Punt on the Red Sea that came back with myrrh trees, ebony and live baboons, all carved on her temple walls. Later rulers chiselled her name away, which is why her reign was rediscovered only in the nineteenth century.

events.title: Akhenaten imposes the worship of the Aten
events.summary: Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, closed the temples of Amun, raised a new capital at Akhetaten in the desert and made the sun disc, the Aten, the only god worth worshipping. Art changed with the theology: elongated bodies, the royal family shown embracing, hymns addressed to light itself. The experiment died with him. His successors abandoned the city, restored the old gods and struck his name from the king lists, and his young son Tutankhamun moved the court back to Thebes.

events.title: Egypt and the Hittites fight at Kadesh
events.summary: On the Orontes in Syria, Ramesses II marched into a Hittite ambush and very nearly lost his army before a relief division saved him. It is probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and it is the earliest battle whose course historians can reconstruct in detail, because both sides left accounts. Ramesses had his version carved across Egypt as a personal triumph; the Hittite records read rather differently, and the frontier in fact stayed where it was.

events.title: The first surviving international peace treaty
events.summary: Sixteen years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III settled their rivalry in writing: no further aggression, mutual defence, and the return of fugitives, with the gods of both kingdoms called as witnesses. It survives twice over, in Egyptian hieroglyphs on temple walls and on Akkadian clay tablets from the Hittite capital, so the two texts can be compared. It is the oldest peace treaty whose full text we have, and a replica hangs at the United Nations.

events.title: The Merneptah Stele names Israel for the first time
events.summary: A granite victory inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah, found at Thebes in 1896, lists the peoples he claims to have crushed in Canaan and includes one written with the hieroglyphic sign for a people rather than a place: Israel. It is the earliest known mention of Israel anywhere, and it puts a group of that name in the southern Levant around 1208 BCE. What the name covered then — a tribe, a confederation, a region — the stele does not say, and archaeologists still argue about it.

events.title: Byblos trades cedar for papyrus and names the book
events.summary: The oldest of the Phoenician ports shipped Lebanese cedar to treeless Egypt for pharaonic barges and coffins and took Egyptian papyrus back in exchange, then sold it on to the Aegean. The Greeks called the writing material after the town — byblos — and from that word come bible and bibliography. Byblos also carries the earliest long inscription in the Phoenician alphabet, on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram, and has been occupied more or less continuously for seven thousand years.

events.title: Ironworking becomes widespread
events.summary: Smelted iron was known in Anatolia by the second millennium BCE, and after about 1200 BCE, as Mediterranean trade in tin faltered, iron tools and weapons spread through the Near East, India and Europe. Iron ore is common, so metal tools became cheap enough for ordinary farmers. Sub-Saharan Africa developed ironworking on its own, with furnaces in Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania dated to the first millennium BCE, a chronology still being refined by new excavations.

events.title: Shang diviners write on oracle bones
events.summary: At Anyang, Shang kings put questions to their ancestors — about harvests, childbirth, hunting and war — by heating ox shoulder blades and turtle shells until they cracked, then had the question and sometimes the outcome carved beside the crack. Farmers were selling the bones as dragon bones for medicine when scholars recognised the marks in 1899. Some 150,000 pieces are known, the earliest substantial Chinese writing, and their characters are recognisably the ancestors of those in use today.

events.title: The Olmec civilisation flourishes
events.summary: Along the Gulf coast of Mexico the Olmec built ceremonial centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta from about 1200 BCE, carving colossal basalt heads and creating a religious imagery of jaguars and rulers that later Mesoamerican peoples inherited. They may have devised the ritual ballgame and early forms of the Long Count calendar and writing, though the earliest datable examples come from their successors. Often called Mesoamerica's mother culture, a label archaeologists debate.

events.title: Phoenicians found Gadir beyond the Mediterranean
events.summary: Sailors from Tyre planted a trading colony on an Atlantic island past the Strait of Gibraltar to reach Iberian silver and tin, and the Spanish city of Cádiz has stood there ever since — by tradition the oldest continuously inhabited city in western Europe. The classical foundation date of about 1100 BCE comes from ancient authors; excavated material so far reaches the ninth century. The colony marks the point at which Phoenician trade left the enclosed Mediterranean for the open ocean.

events.title: The Phoenician alphabet
events.summary: Merchants of the Levantine coast standardised a script of 22 consonant letters around 1050 BCE, descended from earlier Semitic signs used by Canaanite workers in Egypt's Sinai mines. Because it needed only a couple of dozen symbols rather than hundreds, it could be learned quickly. Carried on Phoenician ships, it was adapted by the Greeks, who added vowels, and from them by the Etruscans and Romans; Aramaic, Hebrew, Arabic and the Brahmi scripts of India descend from the same family.

events.title: Zoroaster and the origins of Zoroastrianism
events.summary: Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran whose hymns, the Gathas, form the core of the Avesta, is dated by scholars anywhere between about 1500 and 600 BCE; the language of the Gathas suggests the earlier end. His teaching of one creator god, Ahura Mazda, a cosmic struggle between truth and lie, individual judgment and a final renewal of the world influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Zoroastrianism was the state religion of three Persian empires.

events.title: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, the first empire of its scale
events.summary: From northern Iraq the Assyrian kings built a machine for conquest: a standing army with iron weapons and siege engines, provinces under appointed governors, a royal road and relay messengers, and the mass deportation of defeated populations to break their capacity to revolt. At its height under Ashurbanipal it ran from Iran to Egypt. Its own brutality is recorded in its palace reliefs. A coalition of Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE and the empire vanished within a decade.

events.title: Chavín de Huántar and early Andean civilisation
events.summary: High in the Peruvian Andes, the ceremonial centre of Chavín de Huántar drew pilgrims from across the region between about 900 and 200 BCE to a temple of stone galleries, water channels and carved deities combining jaguar, serpent and human features. Its religious art and iconography spread widely, an early instance of the cultural unification of the Andes that the Inca would later complete politically. Metalworking in gold and textile technology advanced during the same centuries.

events.title: The kingdom of Urartu rises around Lake Van
events.summary: From its rock-cut capital of Tushpa on Lake Van, the kingdom of Urartu dominates the Armenian highlands for nearly three centuries, building fortresses, irrigation canals still in use today, and a cuneiform bureaucracy that trades blows with Assyria itself. When Urartu falls around 590 BCE its lands and peoples pass to the emerging Armenian identity — Persian inscriptions soon call the same country Armina, and later Armenian tradition remembers Urartian sites such as Van as its own deep past.

events.title: Carthage is founded and comes to rule the western seas
events.summary: Tyrian colonists — legend names Queen Dido — found Carthage on the Tunisian coast around 814 BCE. The city grows into the richest port of the western Mediterranean, running trade circuits to Iberia and, under Hanno the Navigator, exploring the West African coast. Its commercial empire, mercenary armies and famous harbours make it Rome's great rival until the Punic Wars end in its destruction.

events.title: Celtic Europe: the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures
events.summary: From salt-rich Hallstatt and the La Tène lakeshore, Celtic-speaking peoples spread across Europe from Iberia to Anatolia — sacking Rome around 390 BCE and raiding Delphi a century later. Masters of ironwork and swirling curvilinear art, they build hillfort towns and trade deep into the Mediterranean world, but never a single state; conquest by Rome and Germanic expansion leaves their languages surviving on the Atlantic fringe.

events.title: The kingdom of Dʿmt rises in the northern highlands
events.summary: Eight centuries before Aksum, a state with monumental stone temples, irrigation and its own inscriptions occupied what is now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia. The great temple at Yeha, still standing to fourteen metres of dry-fitted sandstone, belongs to it. Its script and some of its gods came from Sabaean south Arabia across the Red Sea, and scholars have argued ever since about how much was colonisation and how much local adoption; the present view leans strongly to an indigenous society borrowing selectively.

events.title: The first recorded Olympic Games are held
events.summary: Greek tradition dates the first Olympic festival at Olympia to 776 BCE, and the victor lists that begin there become the backbone of Greek chronology — historians dated events by Olympiads. Held every four years in honour of Zeus, the games drew athletes from every Greek city under a sacred truce, and champions in the sprint, wrestling and chariot race won olive crowns and lasting fame. Suppressed under Christian emperors around 393 CE, they were revived as the modern Olympics in 1896.

events.title: The Iliad and the Odyssey are written down
events.summary: Generations of oral poets had sung of a war at Troy in formulaic verse before someone, or several someones, fixed two long poems in the newly adopted alphabet around the eighth century BCE. The Greeks called the author Homer and knew almost nothing about him. The poems became the shared text of the Greek world — quoted in court, taught to children, argued over by philosophers — and through Rome they became the model for European epic. Whether one poet composed both is still disputed.

events.title: Babylonian astronomers make the sky predictable
events.summary: Scribes in Babylon kept nightly records of the moon, the planets and eclipses for something like seven centuries, the longest continuous observation programme in history, and then used them. They divided the ecliptic into twelve equal signs, isolated the eighteen-year saros cycle of eclipse repetition, and wrote arithmetical schemes that predicted lunar and planetary positions in advance. Hipparchus and Ptolemy built on their tables, and the sexagesimal base they used survives in the sixty minutes of every hour and the 360 degrees of a circle.

events.title: Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh
events.summary: The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, literate himself and proud of it, gathers over thirty thousand cuneiform tablets at Nineveh — omens, medicine, mathematics, letters, and the Epic of Gilgamesh. When the city burns in 612 BCE the clay is baked hard rather than destroyed, accidentally preserving the ancient Near East's greatest single archive. Its nineteenth-century excavation, including the flood tablet, transforms knowledge of the pre-classical world.

events.title: Judaism and the Hebrew Bible take shape
events.summary: The religion of ancient Israel developed into Judaism, centred on one God and the Torah, during and after the Babylonian exile of the sixth century BCE, when much of the Hebrew Bible reached the form we know; scholars date its final editing to the Persian period, around 500 to 400 BCE. Traditions of Abraham and Moses are far older but cannot be dated historically. Judaism's scriptures, ethics and monotheism underlie Christianity and Islam.

events.title: Jerusalem falls and Judah is deported to Babylon
events.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II's army took Jerusalem, burned Solomon's temple and marched the kingdom of Judah's elite to Babylonia. Half a century of exile without a temple or a king forced a religion of sacrifice to become one of text, prayer and assembly, and much of the Hebrew Bible was edited into shape in that period. When Cyrus of Persia allowed a return after 538 BCE, some went back to rebuild the temple and many stayed, beginning a diaspora that has existed ever since.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilds Babylon and its Ishtar Gate
events.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II spent the loot of an empire on his capital: double walls, a processional way, the ziggurat later remembered as the Tower of Babel, and a northern gate faced in lapis-blue glazed brick with rows of moulded bulls and dragons. The glaze technology alone was a serious industrial achievement. A reconstruction from excavated bricks stands in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. The hanging gardens ascribed to the same reign have never been found and may belong to Nineveh instead.

events.title: Cyrus the Great founds the Achaemenid Empire
events.summary: Cyrus, a vassal king in Fars, overthrew his Median overlord in 550 BCE and in twenty years took Lydia and Babylon as well, assembling the largest empire the world had yet seen — from the Aegean to the Indus. Its method was as notable as its size: conquered peoples kept their gods, laws and languages under Persian satraps, and Aramaic served as the administrative tongue across it. At its height under Darius and Xerxes it ruled perhaps two in five people then alive.

events.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
events.summary: After capturing Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great of Persia had a clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian recording his restoration of temples and the return of displaced peoples to their homelands, a policy the Hebrew Bible credits with ending the Jewish exile. It follows Mesopotamian conventions of royal proclamation rather than declaring universal rights, and its modern reputation as the first charter of human rights is disputed by historians. It remains a notable early statement of religious tolerance by a conqueror.

events.title: The Hebrew Bible takes shape after the Babylonian exile
events.summary: After Cyrus permits the Judean exiles to return from Babylon, priests and scribes — tradition names Ezra — assemble law, prophecy and history into the core of the Hebrew Bible. Exile has transformed a national cult into something portable: a religion of text, covenant and congregation that can survive without king or temple. That template of scriptural monotheism will shape Judaism, Christianity and Islam alike.

events.title: Darius I organises the empire: satrapies and the Royal Road
events.summary: Darius I divides the Achaemenid realm into taxed satrapies, standardises coinage on the gold daric, digs a canal joining the Nile to the Red Sea, and builds the Royal Road, whose relay riders cover the 2,700 kilometres from Sardis to Susa in about a week. Herodotus's admiring line about couriers stopped by neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night still rings, via a New York post office, today.

events.title: Rome expels its kings and founds the Republic
events.summary: Tradition dates to 509 BCE the expulsion of Tarquin the Proud and Rome's oath never again to suffer a king. Power passes to paired annual consuls checked by the Senate and, after plebeian struggle, by tribunes with a veto — a constitution of balanced, term-limited magistracies that Polybius will analyse and America's founders will study. The Twelve Tables, published about 450 BCE, make Roman law public property.

events.title: Cleisthenes founds Athenian democracy
events.summary: In 508 BCE the Athenian reformer Cleisthenes reorganised the citizen body into ten tribes and gave the assembly of all adult male citizens the final say over law and war, creating the system later called democracy. Offices were filled by lot, and juries of hundreds judged cases. It excluded women, slaves and resident foreigners, a majority of the population, yet its principle that citizens rule themselves directly became a reference point for every later republic.

events.title: Confucius teaches in China
events.summary: Kong Qiu, known in the West as Confucius, taught in the state of Lu during the late sixth and early fifth centuries BCE, in a period of political fragmentation. His emphasis on ritual propriety, filial duty, learning and humane government was compiled by followers in the Analects. Adopted as state doctrine under the Han dynasty, Confucian thought organised education, the civil service examinations and family life in China for two millennia and deeply influenced Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

events.title: Hanno the Navigator sails down the African coast
events.summary: A Carthaginian expedition took a fleet through the Strait of Gibraltar and south along the Atlantic shore of Africa, planting colonies on the Moroccan coast and reporting drums in the night, a mountain of fire and hairy people its interpreters called gorillae. The account survives only in a short Greek translation of a temple inscription at Carthage. How far it reached — Sierra Leone, Gabon, or no further than southern Morocco — has been argued over for two centuries and is not settled.

events.title: Siddhartha Gautama teaches; Buddhism begins
events.summary: Siddhartha Gautama, later the Buddha, taught in the Ganges plain of northern India in about the fifth century BCE; scholars place his death anywhere between roughly 480 and 400 BCE, so the century is firm and the decades are not. His teaching of a middle path, the four noble truths and release from suffering spread across Asia along trade routes, taking distinct Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana forms and shaping the art, ethics and politics of dozens of societies.

events.title: The Greco-Persian Wars
events.summary: Between 499 and 449 BCE the Achaemenid Persian Empire, the largest state the world had yet seen, fought the Greek city-states. Persian invasions were turned back at Marathon in 490 and, after the sacrifice at Thermopylae, at sea off Salamis in 480 and on land at Plataea in 479. The wars gave Athens its navy and its empire, and Herodotus's account of them is the first surviving work of history. Persia remained the dominant power of the Near East for another 150 years.

events.title: Rome publishes the Twelve Tables
events.summary: Plebeians who could be judged by patrician magistrates applying unwritten custom demanded the law be written down. A commission produced ten tables, then two more, inscribed on bronze and set up in the Forum: procedure, debt, family, inheritance, property and injury, in terse and often harsh clauses. The text is lost and known only through quotation, but Roman schoolboys still learned it by heart centuries later, and it is the root of a legal tradition that reached most of the modern world.

events.title: Athens builds the Parthenon
events.summary: Pericles spent the tribute of Athens's allies on rebuilding the Acropolis the Persians had burned, and Iktinos, Kallikrates and the sculptor Pheidias produced a marble temple to Athena in which almost no line is straight: the columns swell and lean inward and the platform curves, corrections made so the building looks regular to the eye. Its frieze ran 160 metres. It served as a church and then a mosque, and was wrecked in 1687 when a Venetian shell hit the Ottoman powder store inside it.

events.title: The Peloponnesian War breaks Athens
events.summary: For twenty-seven years Athens and its maritime empire fight Sparta and its allies in a war that consumes the Greek world — plague kills Pericles and a third of Athens, a whole Athenian fleet and army are destroyed at Syracuse, and in 404 BCE the starved city surrenders and its walls are pulled down. Thucydides, an exiled Athenian general, chronicles it as 'a possession for all time': the founding work of critical history and of hard-nosed political realism.

events.title: Hippocratic medicine
events.summary: Hippocrates of Kos and the physicians who wrote under his name around 400 BCE treated disease as a natural process with natural causes, to be understood by careful observation of the patient rather than attributed to the gods. The Hippocratic Corpus describes case histories, prognosis and the ethics later distilled into the Hippocratic Oath. Its humoral theory was wrong, and persisted for two thousand years, but its method of observation and its professional ethics are the roots of clinical medicine.

events.title: Gauls defeat Rome at the Allia and sack the city
events.summary: A Senonian war band under Brennus broke a Roman army on the Allia a few miles north of the city and then walked into Rome itself, holding it for months until paid to leave — the occasion of the legend that Brennus threw his sword onto the scales and said woe to the vanquished. It was the only time Rome fell to a foreign enemy for eight centuries, and it shaped Roman fear of the Gauls and the rebuilding of the city's walls. Ancient sources date it 390 or 387 BCE.

events.title: Panini writes the first formal grammar
events.summary: In Gandhara, in what is now Pakistan, Panini described Sanskrit in about four thousand terse rules that generate the language's words and sentences from roots and affixes, with a metalanguage, ordered rule application and explicit conventions for resolving conflicts. Nothing of comparable rigour appears anywhere else before the nineteenth century. Twentieth-century linguists found his system close to what formal grammars and computer languages later required, and his work is still the reference description of classical Sanskrit. His dates are uncertain within a century or two.

events.title: Aristotle founds the Lyceum and maps the sciences
events.summary: After twenty years with Plato and a spell tutoring the young Alexander, Aristotle opened his own school in Athens and set about dividing knowledge into fields — logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, poetics — and writing the first systematic treatise on each. He dissected animals, classified several hundred species, and invented formal logic, which stood essentially unchanged for two thousand years. His physics was wrong and held Europe up for centuries; his method of observation and classification underlies the sciences that corrected him.

events.title: Alexander the Great's conquests
events.summary: In eleven years from 334 BCE Alexander of Macedon destroyed the Persian Empire, took Egypt, marched through Central Asia and fought in the Punjab before his army refused to go further. He died in Babylon in 323 aged 32, and his generals carved his conquests into kingdoms. The Hellenistic world they ruled spread Greek language, cities, science and art from the Mediterranean to Afghanistan, and brought Greek and Indian, Persian and Egyptian ideas into lasting contact.

events.title: Alexander takes Tyre by building a causeway to it
events.summary: Tyre, the leading Phoenician city, sat on an island half a kilometre offshore and refused Alexander entry. He spent seven months driving a stone mole out from the mainland under fire, borrowed a fleet from the other Phoenician ports, and stormed the walls. The city was sacked, its people killed or enslaved. The causeway silted up and permanently joined Tyre to the coast, where it still is; Phoenician independence in the homeland ended with the siege.

events.title: Alexander topples the Achaemenids; Persepolis burns
events.summary: After Gaugamela, Alexander of Macedon takes the Persian capitals; in 330 BCE the ceremonial city of Persepolis is burned — accident, revenge for Athens, or drunken impulse, the sources disagree. The Achaemenid dynasty ends with Darius III's murder, but Persian administration, roads and satrapal governance are absorbed wholesale by Alexander and his successors, carrying the empire's machinery into the Hellenistic world.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya builds India's first great empire
events.summary: Advised by the strategist Chanakya, Chandragupta overthrew the Nanda dynasty at Magadha, took the Indus provinces Alexander's successors had left, and defeated Seleucus, who ceded territory and sent an ambassador. The empire he assembled ran from Bengal to Afghanistan and was administered from Pataliputra by a bureaucracy, a treasury and a spy network of the kind the Arthashastra describes. Jain tradition has him abdicating and fasting to death as an ascetic. His grandson was Ashoka.

events.title: Rome builds the road network that holds the empire together
events.summary: The censor Appius Claudius began the Via Appia south from Rome in 312 BCE, and over the following five centuries the system grew to perhaps eighty thousand kilometres of surveyed, drained and paved highway from Scotland to the Euphrates. Roads were laid in layers on a prepared bed, cambered for drainage, marked with milestones, and served by relay stations for the imperial post. They were built for legions, but they carried trade, tax, law and Christianity, and many modern European routes still follow their lines.

events.title: El Mirador, a Maya city before the Classic age
events.summary: Deep in the Guatemalan rainforest, centuries before the Classic cities, the Maya built El Mirador, whose La Danta complex is among the largest structures by volume ever raised anywhere. Raised limestone causeways ran for kilometres between it and neighbouring centres, and painted friezes there show scenes from the Popol Vuh creation story more than a thousand years before it was written down. The city was largely abandoned by about 150 CE, possibly after deforestation for lime plaster ruined its farmland.

events.title: Euclid's Elements
events.summary: Working in Alexandria around 300 BCE, Euclid organised the geometry and number theory of earlier Greek mathematicians into thirteen books that begin from definitions, postulates and common notions and prove each proposition from what came before. The Elements set the standard of mathematical proof and was the basic geometry textbook for over two thousand years, in Greek, Arabic, Latin and every modern language. Almost nothing is known of Euclid himself; even his dates are inferred.

events.title: The Library and Museum of Alexandria
events.summary: Under the early Ptolemies, Alexandria's Museum and its library set out to collect every text in the world, holding perhaps hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Here Euclid systematises geometry, Eratosthenes measures the Earth's circumference, Aristarchus proposes a sun-centred cosmos, and Herophilus dissects the human body. Its slow decline — not one dramatic fire — has made it the enduring symbol of knowledge lost.

events.title: Celts settle in Anatolia and become the Galatians
events.summary: Three Celtic tribes invited across the Bosphorus as mercenaries stayed, carved out a territory around modern Ankara and lived there as a self-governing people with their own council of tetrarchs for centuries, raiding and hiring themselves out to the Hellenistic kings. They kept a Celtic language into the fourth century CE, further east than any other Celtic speech reached. Paul's letter to the Galatians is addressed to their descendants, and it is the reason a Celtic people's name is familiar to most readers of the New Testament.

events.title: The Punic Wars
events.summary: Rome and Carthage fought three wars between 264 and 146 BCE for control of the western Mediterranean. In the second, Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and destroyed Roman armies at Cannae, yet Rome refused to yield and won in Africa at Zama in 202. The third ended with Carthage razed and its territory made a Roman province. Victory left Rome the dominant power of the Mediterranean and set it on the road from republic to empire.

events.title: Ashoka's edicts
events.summary: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga around 260 BCE, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka renounced war and had edicts carved on rocks and pillars across the Indian subcontinent, from Afghanistan to the Deccan, in Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic. They proclaim dhamma, a policy of non-violence, religious tolerance, care for the sick, prisoners and animals, and just administration, and describe the emperor's own remorse. They are the earliest surviving royal inscriptions of India and a rare ancient statement of governance by ethical principle.

events.title: Archimedes and the mathematics of machines
events.summary: Archimedes of Syracuse, who died when the Romans took the city in 212 BCE, worked out the law of the lever, the principle of buoyancy that bears his name, the volume and surface of the sphere, and a method of exhaustion that anticipated integral calculus. He designed compound pulleys and the water-raising screw and, by tradition, war machines to defend Syracuse. His surviving treatises, recovered partly from a palimpsest, show a mathematical physicist working eighteen centuries before Galileo.

events.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
events.summary: The chief librarian at Alexandria knew that at midsummer noon the sun stood directly over a well at Syene, while at Alexandria it cast a shadow about a fiftieth of a circle from vertical. Multiplying the distance between the cities by fifty gave him the circumference of the globe. Depending on the length of his stadion the result is within a few per cent of the true 40,000 kilometres. He also drew the first map with lines of latitude and longitude and invented a method for sieving out prime numbers.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China
events.summary: In 221 BCE the king of Qin completed the conquest of the six rival Warring States and proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor. He standardised the script, weights, measures, coinage and axle widths, built roads and canals, linked earlier walls into a northern frontier, and was buried with the terracotta army near Xi'an. His dynasty fell four years after his death, but the unified, centrally administered empire he created became the enduring shape of China.

events.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps into Italy
events.summary: Rather than wait for Rome, the Carthaginian general marched from Spain through Gaul and over an Alpine pass in autumn with an army and war elephants, losing many of both on the way. In Italy he destroyed Roman armies at Trebia, Lake Trasimene and finally Cannae in 216 BCE, where his double envelopment of a much larger force is still taught in staff colleges. He held the peninsula for fifteen years without taking Rome, and was recalled to defeat at Zama.

events.title: Celtic Europe builds towns: the oppida
events.summary: In the last two centuries BCE, temperate Europe north of the Alps filled with large fortified settlements — Manching, Bibracte, Gergovia — enclosed by timber-laced ramparts and containing workshops, coin mints, iron and glass production and planned streets. Some covered hundreds of hectares. They were the first towns in Europe north of the Mediterranean world, evidence of a Celtic society with markets, currency and specialists, which is not the picture the Roman accounts of barbarian Gaul encouraged.

events.title: Rome destroys Carthage
events.summary: Fifty years after Carthage had been disarmed, Rome demanded that the city be abandoned and rebuilt inland. The Carthaginians refused and withstood a three-year siege before Scipio Aemilianus took the place street by street and burned it. The survivors were sold into slavery and the territory became the Roman province of Africa. The story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt is a nineteenth-century invention. Phoenician culture survived in North Africa for centuries afterwards, but its last independent state was gone.

events.title: Zhang Qian and the opening of the Silk Road
events.summary: Sent west by the Han emperor Wu in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu, the envoy Zhang Qian was captured, escaped, and returned thirteen years later with the first Chinese accounts of Central Asia, Bactria and Persia. His reports led the Han to push into the Tarim Basin and open regular trade with the west. The routes later called the Silk Road carried silk, horses, glass, religions, technologies and, at times, plague between China, India, Persia and Rome.

events.title: Tigranes the Great builds an Armenian empire
events.summary: Tigranes II takes the Armenian throne in 95 BCE and for a generation makes Armenia the strongest state in the Roman East, stretching from the Caspian to the Mediterranean and taking the Persian title 'king of kings'. He founds a new capital, Tigranocerta, populated by transplanted Greek craftsmen. Rome's generals Lucullus and Pompey eventually strip the conquests away, but the empire fixes Armenia's self-image: a nation that was once, briefly, the centre of its world.

events.title: Spartacus leads a slave war against Rome
events.summary: A Thracian gladiator broke out of a training school at Capua with some seventy others and within two years commanded tens of thousands of escaped slaves, beating consular armies twice and ranging the length of Italy. Crassus finally penned and destroyed the force in 71 BCE and had six thousand survivors crucified along the road to Rome. It was the third and largest of Rome's slave wars and the last; the revolt changed nothing legally, but it fixed itself in the European imagination as the archetype of revolt.

events.title: Vercingetorix surrenders at Alesia and Gaul falls
events.summary: Vercingetorix had united a large part of Gaul against Caesar and beaten him at Gergovia before being shut up in the hill fort of Alesia. Caesar built two rings of siege works, one facing in and one facing out, and held both against the garrison and a huge relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered to save his people and was paraded in Rome and executed six years later. Independent Celtic Gaul ended there, and Gaul became the richest group of provinces in the western empire.

events.title: Glassblowing is invented on the Phoenician coast
events.summary: Somewhere around Sidon and Jerusalem in the first century BCE, craftsmen discovered that a blob of molten glass on the end of a hollow iron tube could be inflated into a vessel. Glass stopped being a luxury ground and cast like stone and became something a workshop could turn out by the hundred. Within a generation Roman households were drinking from it and storing food in it, and Sidonian blowers signed their work. The technique is still, in essence, how glass is shaped by hand.

events.title: Julius Caesar is assassinated; the Roman Empire follows
events.summary: Julius Caesar, who had crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and won a civil war to become dictator, was stabbed to death by senators on the Ides of March, 44 BCE. His death did not restore the republic: thirteen more years of civil war ended with his heir Octavian defeating Antony and Cleopatra and taking the name Augustus in 27 BCE as the first emperor. The Roman Empire he founded ruled the Mediterranean world for the next four centuries.

events.title: The Long Count fixes a date on a Mesoamerican calendar
events.summary: Mesoamerican scribes counted days continuously from a mythical starting point in 3114 BCE, writing the total in a positional system with a symbol for zero — one of the few independent inventions of zero in history. The earliest surviving Long Count dates, on stelae at Chiapa de Corzo and Tres Zapotes, fall in the first century BCE. The Maya combined it with a 260-day ritual round and a 365-day year, and calculated Venus cycles and eclipses accurately centuries ahead.

events.title: Cleopatra's death ends three thousand years of pharaohs
events.summary: Cleopatra VII, last of the Macedonian Ptolemies and the only one who reportedly learned Egyptian, tried to keep her kingdom independent by allying with Caesar and then with Mark Antony. Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BCE ended that; a year later both she and Antony were dead and Egypt became a Roman province governed as the emperor's private grain estate. Native Egyptian kingship, already three millennia old, stopped there, though the temples and the hieroglyphs carried on for another four centuries.

events.title: Augustus founds the Roman Empire
events.summary: Octavian, victor of the civil wars that consumed the Republic, returns his powers to the Senate in 27 BCE and receives them back with the new name Augustus — monarchy wearing republican clothes. His settlement brings two centuries of internal peace, a professional army on the frontiers, a census-based administration, and an imperial cult; the title Caesar becomes a word for ruler in languages from German to Russian.

events.title: The ministry of Jesus; Christianity begins
events.summary: Jesus of Nazareth taught in Galilee and Judea and was executed by the Roman authorities in Jerusalem around 30 CE; the exact year is uncertain within a few years either side. His followers, first a movement within Judaism, spread his message through the Roman Empire, aided by Paul's letters and the Greek-speaking cities of the eastern Mediterranean. Three centuries later Christianity was tolerated and then adopted by the empire, becoming the largest religion in the world today.

events.title: Boudica leads the British revolt against Rome
events.summary: When Rome annexes the Iceni kingdom, flogs its widowed queen Boudica and assaults her daughters, she raises the Celtic tribes of Britain in revolt. Her armies burn the Roman towns of Camulodunum, Verulamium and the young trading post of Londinium, killing tens of thousands, before the outnumbered legions annihilate the rebels in a final pitched battle. Boudica's death ends Celtic resistance in lowland Britain, but Tacitus' account makes her an enduring symbol of defiance against empire.

events.title: Rome destroys the Second Temple; the diaspora deepens
events.summary: Titus's legions storm Jerusalem in 70 CE, ending the great Jewish revolt and burning the Second Temple; the menorah is paraded through Rome on the Arch of Titus. Sacrificial religion centred on one sanctuary gives way, under the rabbis of Yavneh and their successors, to synagogue, study and the Mishnah — the durable, dispersed Judaism of the following two millennia.

events.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum
events.summary: A column of ash and pumice rose over the Bay of Naples and then collapsed into pyroclastic surges that killed those who had stayed and sealed two towns under metres of debris. Pliny the Younger's letters describing it gave volcanology the term Plinian eruption. Because the burial was instantaneous, Pompeii preserves what no other Roman site does — painted walls, graffiti, shop counters, loaves in ovens, and casts of the dead made by pouring plaster into the voids their bodies left in the ash.

events.title: Funan and the port of Oc Eo
events.summary: The first state known in mainland Southeast Asia sat on the Mekong delta and lived off the trade passing between India and China. Its port at Oc Eo has yielded Roman coins, Indian seals and Chinese mirrors in the same layers, and a canal network tens of kilometres long. Funan took in Sanskrit, Hindu gods and Indian notions of kingship and passed them to its successors. It is known mainly through Chinese embassies' reports, and its relationship to the later Khmer is debated.

events.title: Teotihuacan rises
events.summary: Northeast of modern Mexico City, Teotihuacan grew after 100 CE into one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 people, a grid plan, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and apartment compounds housing craft workers and migrants from across Mesoamerica. Its influence reached the Maya cities, where its warriors intervened in 378. The city burned around 550 in circumstances still debated. Its builders' name for it and their language are unknown.

events.title: Papermaking is perfected in Han China
events.summary: The court official Cai Lun reported an improved papermaking process to the Han emperor in 105 CE, using bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets; archaeology shows cruder paper in China a century or two earlier, so he standardised rather than invented it. Paper was far cheaper than silk or bamboo strips and spread with Buddhism to Korea and Japan, reached the Islamic world after 751, and Europe by the twelfth century, where it made printing economical.

events.title: Under Trajan the Roman Empire reaches its greatest extent
events.summary: Trajan's conquest of Dacia paid for a building programme — a new forum, markets, a harbour at Ostia, roads and bridges — and his Parthian campaign carried Roman standards to the Persian Gulf, the furthest they ever went. The empire then covered some five million square kilometres and perhaps a fifth of humanity. His successor Hadrian abandoned the eastern gains at once as indefensible. Trajan's Column still stands in Rome, its spiral relief the best surviving picture of the Roman army at work.

events.title: The Pantheon's concrete dome
events.summary: Hadrian's rebuilt temple to all the gods is roofed by an unreinforced concrete dome 43 metres across, lightened towards the top by coffering and by graded aggregate — heavy travertine at the base, light pumice at the crown — and opened at the centre by a nine-metre oculus. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, nineteen centuries on. Continuous use as a church from 609 saved it, and it taught Brunelleschi, Michelangelo and Jefferson what concrete and a dome could do.

events.title: The Bar Kokhba revolt and the loss of Judaea
events.summary: Sixty years after the temple's destruction, Simon bar Kokhba led a second rising against Rome, ran an independent administration long enough to mint its own coins, and was hailed as messiah by Rabbi Akiva. Hadrian committed legions from across the empire to crush it. The defeat was catastrophic: hundreds of settlements destroyed, Jews barred from Jerusalem, and the province renamed Syria Palaestina. Jewish life moved to Galilee and Babylonia, where the rabbinic academies produced the Mishnah and the Talmud.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest
events.summary: Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria around 150 CE, compiled Greek and Babylonian astronomy into a mathematical model of an Earth-centred cosmos that predicted planetary positions well enough to remain the standard for 1,400 years, in Greek, Arabic and Latin. His Geography, with its coordinates of thousands of places, guided mapmakers into the age of Columbus. The Almagest was wrong about the Earth's place, but its demand that theory match measured positions made it the model of quantitative science.

events.title: The runic alphabet is cut into wood, bone and stone
events.summary: Germanic speakers adapted an alphabet, probably from an Italic script, into twenty-four angular characters designed to be carved across the grain of wood — which is why runes avoid horizontal and curved strokes. The elder futhark appears on weapons, combs and memorial stones from the second century on. A shortened sixteen-rune version served the Viking Age, leaving thousands of inscriptions in Scandinavia recording the dead, voyages, debts and jokes, and runes were still used in rural Sweden into the nineteenth century.

events.title: The Mishnah and the Talmud are compiled
events.summary: With no temple, Judaism reorganised around law and argument. Around 200 CE Judah the Prince edited the oral traditions into the Mishnah, a terse code in Hebrew; over the next four centuries the academies of Galilee and Mesopotamia layered commentary on it, and the Babylonian version became the Talmud. It preserves minority opinions beside majority rulings, which makes it a record of reasoning rather than a statute book, and it has been the central text of rabbinic study ever since.

events.title: Caracalla makes almost every free subject a Roman citizen
events.summary: By a single edict the emperor Caracalla extended citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire, some thirty million people who had until then been subjects governed by local law. Contemporaries suspected the motive was tax, since citizens paid inheritance duty. The effect was to make Roman civil law the common law of the Mediterranean world and to dissolve the old distinction between conqueror and conquered — one reason Roman identity outlasted the western empire by so long.

events.title: Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire
events.summary: Ardashir I, a local ruler from Persis, defeats the last Parthian king at Hormozdgan in 224 and crowns himself shahanshah — king of kings — restoring a centralised Persian empire that will fight Rome and Byzantium to a standstill for four centuries. The Sasanians make Zoroastrianism a state church, build the great academy at Gundeshapur, and set the imperial style that the caliphate later inherits. Their exhausting last war with Byzantium opens the door to the Arab conquests.

events.title: Classic Maya civilization flourishes
events.summary: City-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán raise pyramids above the rainforest, wage dynastic wars recorded in the Americas' only fully developed writing system, and track Venus and eclipses with calendars of remarkable precision — including a place-value count using zero. Around 900 the southern cities empty in a drought-linked collapse, but Maya peoples, languages and books continue in the north and endure today.

events.title: The Classic Maya and their collapse
events.summary: Between about 250 and 900 CE Maya city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Copán and Palenque raised stone pyramids, recorded their kings' wars and rituals in the only fully developed writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, and computed calendars and astronomical cycles with great precision. In the ninth century the southern lowland cities were abandoned one after another; drought, warfare, overpopulation and political failure are all implicated, in a mix still debated. Maya society continued in the north and survives today.

events.title: Shapur I captures a Roman emperor
events.summary: At Edessa the Sasanian king Shapur I defeated a Roman field army and took the emperor Valerian alive, the only time Rome lost a reigning emperor to a foreign enemy. Shapur had the scene cut into the cliff faces at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur, with the emperor kneeling before his horse. Captured Roman engineers were resettled to build bridges and dams in Khuzestan. The rock reliefs fixed Sasanian Iran's claim to be Rome's equal rather than its frontier problem.

events.title: Japan's Yamato state emerges from the Kofun age
events.summary: Enormous keyhole-shaped burial mounds — the largest, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is longer than the Great Pyramid is tall — mark the rise of the Yamato line that still occupies Japan's throne, the world's oldest continuing monarchy. Horses, writing and Buddhism arrive via Korea; by the seventh century Prince Shōtoku's court is issuing constitutions and embassies modelled on China while remaining decisively Japanese.

events.title: Armenia becomes the first Christian state
events.summary: King Tiridates III, converted by Gregory the Illuminator, makes Christianity Armenia's state religion around 301 — a decade before Constantine's edict of toleration and generations before Rome itself converts. The cathedral at Etchmiadzin, founded soon after, still serves the Armenian Apostolic Church. Wedged between Rome and Persia, Armenia binds its national identity to its church so tightly that seventeen centuries of empire and diaspora never dissolve it.

events.title: The Edict of Milan legalises Christianity
events.summary: Meeting at Milan in 313, the emperors Constantine and Licinius agree to tolerate every religion in the empire, ending the persecution of Christians and restoring their confiscated property. Constantine, victorious the year before under a Christian sign at the Milvian Bridge, goes further: imperial patronage builds churches, convenes the Council of Nicaea, and founds Constantinople as a Christian capital. Within eighty years Christianity moves from persecuted minority to the official religion of the Roman state.

events.title: Aksum: trading empire and early Christian kingdom
events.summary: The kingdom of Aksum, minting its own gold coinage and raising granite stelae over thirty metres tall, controls Red Sea trade between Rome and India. Around 330 King Ezana converts to Christianity — among the first states anywhere to do so — and the church of Ethiopia begins its unbroken history, complete with its own script, Ge'ez, and a canon that preserves texts lost everywhere else.

events.title: Constantine founds a new Rome on the Bosphorus
events.summary: Constantine refounded the Greek town of Byzantium as his capital, on a peninsula guarded on three sides by water and commanding the crossing between Europe and Asia and the grain route from the Black Sea. He gave it a senate, free bread, and churches instead of the old temples. Theodosius II's landward triple walls, finished in 413, held off every attacker for a thousand years. The city outlived the western empire by almost a millennium and is now Istanbul.

events.title: The Kingdom of Aksum adopts Christianity
events.summary: Aksum, in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, controlled Red Sea trade between Rome and India, minted its own gold coins and raised carved granite stelae over thirty metres tall. Around 330 CE King Ezana converted to Christianity, making Aksum one of the first states to adopt the faith, a decade or so after Armenia and before the Roman Empire did officially. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, with its own script and scriptures, descends directly from this decision.

events.title: Geʽez becomes a vowelled script
events.summary: The consonant-only alphabet Aksum inherited from south Arabia was reworked in the fourth century by adding systematic marks to every letter for the vowel that follows it, producing a syllabary of over two hundred characters. The change is usually connected with the need to write scripture unambiguously after Aksum's conversion. Geʽez remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, and the script it produced is still used daily for Amharic, Tigrinya and Tigre.

events.title: Gupta-era India: zero, decimal numerals and classical science
events.summary: Under and after the Gupta empire, Indian scholars perfect the decimal place-value system with a symbol for zero — the numerals the world now writes. Aryabhata computes pi, treats the day as the Earth's rotation, and models eclipses; Kalidasa writes Sanskrit drama's masterpieces; the universities at Nalanda draw students from across Asia. Transmitted through the Islamic world, these 'Arabic' numerals become the mathematics of everyone.

events.title: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet
events.summary: The monk Mesrop Mashtots devises a thirty-six-letter alphabet fitted precisely to Armenian, and a translation movement immediately renders the Bible and Greek and Syriac learning into the new script — a fifth-century golden age Armenians still celebrate. The alphabet, essentially unchanged, has carried the language through partition, empire and genocide; a holiday honours it, and Mashtots is a saint of the Armenian church.
