events.title: Nalanda becomes a university of the Buddhist world
events.summary: Endowed by Gupta kings in Bihar, Nalanda grew into a residential monastic college of thousands of students and hundreds of teachers, taking entrants by oral examination at the gate and teaching Buddhist philosophy alongside logic, grammar, medicine and mathematics. Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang and Yijing studied there and described its nine-storey library. It drew students from Tibet, Korea, China and Southeast Asia for seven centuries until raiders of the Delhi Sultanate destroyed it around 1200.

events.title: Patrick's mission and the conversion of Ireland
events.summary: A Romano-British teenager carried off by Irish raiders escaped, trained as a cleric and went back as a missionary bishop; his own short Confessio is one of the very few personal documents to survive from fifth-century Britain or Ireland. Christianity took hold in a country Rome had never governed, organised around monasteries rather than cities, and Irish monks then carried literacy back into Britain and the continent. The traditional date of 432 comes from later annals and is not secure.

events.title: Avarayr: Armenia fights for its faith
events.summary: When the Sasanian shah ordered Armenia back to Zoroastrianism, Vardan Mamikonian led a heavily outnumbered army against the imperial force on the Avarayr plain and was killed there. The battle was lost. Guerrilla resistance continued until the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484 conceded Armenians the right to practise Christianity, which is why the defeat is remembered as a victory. Vardan and his companions are saints of the Armenian church, and the day is still observed.

events.title: The Western Roman Empire ends
events.summary: In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople, the date conventionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire after a century of invasions, civil wars and fiscal decline. Historians stress that the transition was gradual: Roman law, cities, Latin and the Church persisted under the Gothic, Frankish and other kingdoms, and the Eastern Empire continued from Constantinople for another thousand years.

events.title: Clovis unites the Franks and is baptised a Catholic
events.summary: Clovis absorbed the other Frankish kingdoms and most of Roman Gaul, and then accepted baptism at Reims as a Catholic rather than as an Arian Christian like every other Germanic king of the day. The choice aligned him with the Gallo-Roman bishops and landowners he now ruled, and it made the Frankish monarchy the church's partner in the west for the next thousand years. He also had Frankish customary law written down as the Salic Law. The baptism's date is uncertain, 496 to 508.

events.title: Indian mathematicians develop the decimal place-value system and zero
events.summary: Indian mathematicians of the Gupta era and after wrote numbers with ten symbols in place-value notation, and in 628 CE Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta gave rules for arithmetic with zero as a number in its own right, including negative numbers and debts. The Bakhshali manuscript, whose leaves have been radiocarbon-dated to between the third and tenth centuries, contains an early dot for zero. Transmitted through the Islamic world, these became the Hindu-Arabic numerals used everywhere today.

events.title: Tiwanaku on the Bolivian altiplano
events.summary: Near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, nearly 4,000 metres above sea level, Tiwanaku grew between about 500 and 1000 CE into a city of monumental platforms, the Gateway of the Sun and precisely fitted stonework, supported by raised-field agriculture that kept crops from freezing. Its influence, with that of contemporary Wari to the north, reached across Bolivia, Peru and Chile. Prolonged drought around 1000 is thought to have brought its decline. The Inca later claimed it as their origin place.

events.title: The Corpus Juris Civilis of Justinian
events.summary: The emperor Justinian ordered Roman law collected, edited and systematised; the Code, Digest and Institutes issued between 529 and 534 preserved a thousand years of Roman legal thought in a form students and courts could use. Rediscovered in Italy in the eleventh century, the Corpus became the foundation of the civil-law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa, and of canon law. Concepts such as contract, property and legal personhood descend from it.

events.title: The academy of Gondishapur gathers the medicine of three worlds
events.summary: In Khuzestan, under Sasanian patronage that peaked with Khosrow I, a teaching hospital and translation centre drew Greek physicians pushed out of Athens and Edessa, Syriac Christian scholars and Indian medical texts into one place, working largely in Syriac. Its graduates staffed the first hospitals of Abbasid Baghdad, and the Bukhtishu family served caliphs as court doctors for generations. Some of the grander claims made for it rest on later sources, but its role as a bridge from Greek and Indian medicine into Islamic science is well founded.

events.title: Justinian builds Hagia Sophia and codifies Roman law
events.summary: In five years Justinian's architects raise Hagia Sophia, its thirty-one-metre dome seeming, in Procopius's words, suspended from heaven — the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a millennium. The same reign distils a thousand years of Roman jurisprudence into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the code through which Roman law reaches medieval Europe and, ultimately, most modern civil-law systems from France to Japan.

events.title: The Plague of Justinian
events.summary: The first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague reached Egypt in 541 and Constantinople in 542, where the historian Procopius described thousands dying daily. Ancient DNA has confirmed the bacterium Yersinia pestis in graves from the period. Older estimates of mortality in the tens of millions have been challenged by recent scholarship, which finds less evidence of demographic collapse than once assumed. Recurrent outbreaks continued until about 750, forming the First Plague Pandemic.

events.title: Chenla succeeds Funan in the Khmer heartland
events.summary: Inland principalities of Khmer speakers along the middle Mekong absorbed Funan and left the earliest inscriptions in the Khmer language, recording temple endowments, land and the labour attached to it. Their brick sanctuaries at Sambor Prei Kuk, set in a walled city, established the architectural vocabulary Angkor would work in stone. Chinese sources describe the polity splitting into land and water halves in the eighth century, and modern scholars doubt it was ever a single kingdom at all.

events.title: Tikal and Calakmul fight for the Maya lowlands
events.summary: Maya politics was not a peaceful theocracy of stargazers. Inscriptions record a defeat of Tikal in 562 that began a hiatus of over a century in its monuments, engineered by Calakmul and its allies, and Tikal's revenge under Jasaw Chan K'awiil in 695, after which it built the great roof-combed temples that stand today. The two superpowers ran rival networks of client kingdoms across the lowlands, and reading their quarrel from the glyphs is one of the achievements of modern archaeology.

events.title: Prince Shotoku issues the Seventeen Articles
events.summary: Regent for his aunt the empress, Shotoku promulgated a set of moral injunctions for officials drawn from Confucian and Buddhist teaching: harmony is to be valued, reverence the three treasures of Buddhism, obey imperial commands, decide matters by discussion and not alone. It is not a constitution in the legal sense but a charter of how a centralised court should behave, and it marks the point at which Japan began deliberately importing Chinese institutions. Its attribution to Shotoku himself is questioned by some historians.

events.title: Muhammad's revelations; Islam begins
events.summary: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad received his first revelation near Mecca in 610 CE and continued to receive the verses later compiled as the Quran until his death in 632. His migration to Medina in 622 marks year one of the Islamic calendar. Within a century of his death Muslim rule stretched from Spain to the Indus, and the faith's law, scholarship, architecture and trade networks linked Africa, Asia and Europe for the next thousand years.

events.title: The Khmer script is first dated
events.summary: An inscription at Angkor Borei bearing a date equivalent to 611 CE is the oldest securely dated writing in Khmer, adapted from the Pallava script of southern India and reshaped for a language with far more vowels than Sanskrit. The script has been written continuously ever since, and Thai and Lao writing both descend from it. Zero also appears on a seventh-century Khmer stone, one of the earliest unambiguous uses of the digit anywhere.

events.title: Pakal's tomb at Palenque
events.summary: K'inich Janaab Pakal ruled the city in the Chiapas hills for 68 years, rebuilding it in a refined architecture of thin walls, mansard roofs and delicate stucco. Beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, reached by a stairway deliberately filled in, Alberto Ruz found his sarcophagus in 1952, its carved lid showing the king falling into the underworld along the world tree. Palenque's long glyphic texts were central to deciphering Maya writing as dynastic history rather than astronomy.

events.title: Tang dynasty China: the cosmopolitan golden age
events.summary: Under the Tang, Chang'an becomes probably the largest city on Earth, home to a million people and to Persian, Sogdian, Korean and Japanese merchants, monks and students. The examination system opens office to talent, Li Bai and Du Fu write the poetry every Chinese schoolchild still learns, woodblock printing spreads the written word, and Tang law and institutions become the model for Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

events.title: The Tang dynasty and Chang'an
events.summary: The Tang dynasty, founded in 618, ruled a China open to the world: its capital Chang'an, with about a million people, was probably the largest city on Earth, home to Persian, Sogdian, Turkic and Indian merchants, Buddhist monks, Nestorian Christians and Muslims. Tang armies reached the Pamirs; Tang poetry, law codes and administration were adopted in Japan, Korea and Vietnam. Woodblock printing appeared in this era. The dynasty declined after the An Lushan rebellion of 755 and fell in 907.

events.title: The Constitution of Medina
events.summary: Arriving in Yathrib from Mecca, Muhammad drew up a written agreement among the emigrants, the city's Arab clans and its Jewish tribes: they formed one community for defence, each group kept its own religion and customary law, blood money and ransom obligations were fixed, and disputes went to the Prophet. It is the founding document of the first Muslim polity and one of the earliest written constitutions anywhere. Its text survives in early biographies, and its status as a single document is debated.

events.title: The early Muslim conquests
events.summary: Within a century of Muhammad's death in 632, Arab armies under the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphs had taken Syria, Egypt and Persia, crossed North Africa into Spain, and reached the Indus and the Talas river in Central Asia. The Sasanian Empire was destroyed and the Byzantine Empire halved. Conquest was not mass conversion; Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians paid a tax and kept their faiths, and Islam became the majority religion in most of these lands only over centuries.

events.title: Qadisiyyah brings down Sasanian Iran
events.summary: An Arab Muslim army beat the Sasanian field force somewhere near Kufa in Iraq, opened the road to the capital Ctesiphon and ended four centuries of Sasanian rule; the last king, Yazdegerd III, was killed on the run in 651. Iran kept its language and much of its administration and later gave Islam a great deal of its science and poetry, but Zoroastrianism shrank to a minority and some of its community eventually settled in India as the Parsis. The year is given variously as 636 or 637.

events.title: Silla unifies the Korean peninsula
events.summary: The smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms allied with Tang China to destroy Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668 — and then spent eight years fighting its ally out of the peninsula, which it managed by 676. The unified state that followed built Gyeongju into a capital of perhaps a million, adopted Buddhism as a state religion, and gave Korea its first single political and cultural frame. Goguryeo's northern territories were lost, and their inheritance is still argued over by Korean and Chinese historians.

events.title: Srivijaya controls the straits
events.summary: From Palembang in Sumatra, a Malay thalassocracy taxed the shipping passing between India and China through the Malacca and Sunda straits for six centuries, holding its coastal vassals by naval power and trade rather than territory. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing stopped there in 671 to learn Sanskrit and found a thousand Buddhist monks, making it a centre of learning as well as commerce. Chola raids in 1025 and shifting trade routes wore it down, and it left few monuments.

events.title: Greek fire saves Constantinople
events.summary: A Syrian refugee named Kallinikos is credited with giving the Byzantine navy an incendiary liquid that could be pumped through a siphon onto enemy ships and that kept burning on water. It broke the Arab fleets besieging Constantinople in the 670s and again in 717. The recipe was a state secret restricted to the emperor and a single family of technicians, and it was lost so completely that its composition — probably a distilled petroleum mixture — is still argued about by chemists and historians.

events.title: The Dome of the Rock is built in Jerusalem
events.summary: The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik raised an octagonal shrine over the rock on Jerusalem's Temple Mount, the oldest Islamic building still standing in anything like its original form. Its mosaics carry the earliest dated Quranic inscriptions in existence, addressed in part to Christians. The same caliph made Arabic the language of administration and struck the first purely epigraphic Islamic coinage. The building is a statement that the new faith intended to stay, in the city all three monotheisms claim.

events.title: Japan's first histories and the Nara court
events.summary: The Kojiki of 712 and Nihon Shoki of 720, compiled at the imperial court, recorded the myths of the kami, the sun goddess Amaterasu and the descent of the imperial line, fixing in writing the traditions later called Shinto, alongside Chinese-style chronicles. The court at Nara, laid out on the model of Chang'an, sponsored Buddhism as well: the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was dedicated in 752. Japan's dual religious tradition of kami and Buddhas dates from this century.

events.title: Constantinople holds against the Umayyad siege
events.summary: An Umayyad army and fleet invested the city for twelve months in a deliberate attempt to finish the Roman empire in the east. Leo III's walls, Greek fire, a hard winter, Bulgarian attacks on the besiegers' camp and desertion among the fleet's Christian crews destroyed the expedition; a small fraction of the ships got home. The failure fixed the frontier in Anatolia for three centuries and is often ranked beside Tours as one of the battles that decided how far the caliphate would reach into Europe.

events.title: Byzantium's iconoclasm controversy
events.summary: For over a century Byzantine emperors ban and destroy religious images, arguing icons are idols; monks and much of the populace resist, and the empire convulses over theology with imperial politics underneath. The final 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' in 843 restores the icons and fixes Eastern Christianity's distinctive devotional art. The dispute deepens the growing estrangement between Constantinople and Rome that will end in the schism of 1054.

events.title: Charles Martel halts an Arab advance at Tours
events.summary: A raiding force from Muslim Spain moving up the Loire was met between Tours and Poitiers by Frankish infantry under Charles Martel, who held his formation and killed the governor Abd al-Rahman. Edward Gibbon made it the battle that saved Christian Europe; modern historians treat it as one check among several on an over-extended frontier. Its certain consequence was domestic: Charles's prestige let his family displace the Merovingian kings, and his grandson was Charlemagne.

events.title: Silla builds Seokguram and Bulguksa
events.summary: Above Gyeongju, Silla masons assembled an artificial grotto from hundreds of fitted granite blocks, roofed it with a corbelled dome and set inside a seated Buddha three and a half metres high, surrounded by relief guardians and bodhisattvas, positioned to face the sunrise over the East Sea. A natural ventilation system kept it dry for twelve centuries until a Japanese-era restoration sealed it. With the temple of Bulguksa below it, it is the high point of Korean Buddhist art.

events.title: Talas halts the Tang and carries paper west
events.summary: Abbasid forces with Tibetan and Karluk allies beat a Tang army on the Talas river in what is now Kyrgyzstan, the only time the two empires met in battle. Tang power west of the Pamirs ended, and Central Asia turned Muslim rather than Chinese. Later Arabic sources say Chinese prisoners taken there included papermakers, and the first paper mill in Samarkand dates from soon after; the causal link is traditional and cannot be proved, but paper did reach Baghdad within decades.

events.title: Nara casts the Great Buddha of Todai-ji
events.summary: Emperor Shomu ordered a bronze Vairocana Buddha nearly sixteen metres high as the centre of a national network of provincial temples, and the casting consumed most of Japan's available copper and, by one account, the labour of two million people. An Indian monk performed the eye-opening ceremony before envoys from across Asia. The wooden hall that shelters it, rebuilt smaller in 1709, is still among the largest timber buildings in the world, and the project nearly bankrupted the Nara state.

events.title: Baghdad founded; the Abbasid golden age
events.summary: Caliph al-Mansur founds round Baghdad on the Tigris in 762; within a century it is among the world's largest and most learned cities. In its House of Wisdom milieu, Greek, Persian and Indian works are translated wholesale into Arabic; al-Khwarizmi writes the book that names algebra, and paper-making, newly arrived from China, makes books cheap. Europe will later relearn much of ancient science through these Arabic channels.

events.title: Borobudur and the Buddhist kingdoms of Java and Sumatra
events.summary: The Sailendra rulers of central Java built Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist monument, around 780 to 830 CE: a stepped pyramid of nine terraces carrying 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues, arranged as a pilgrim's path from the world of desire to enlightenment. Contemporary Srivijaya on Sumatra controlled the straits between India and China and was a centre of Buddhist learning visited by Chinese pilgrims. Both show Southeast Asia adapting Indian religion into its own monumental forms.

events.title: Lindisfarne raid opens the Viking Age
events.summary: Norse raiders sack the island monastery of Lindisfarne in 793, shocking Christian Europe and opening three centuries of Scandinavian expansion. Longships carry Vikings raiding to Paris and Seville, trading down the Russian rivers to Byzantium and the caliphate, and settling Iceland, the Danelaw and Normandy. The same seafaring culture produces assemblies like Iceland's Althing, among the world's oldest parliaments.

events.title: Charlemagne is crowned emperor
events.summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charles, king of the Franks, as emperor in Rome, the first in the West since 476. Charlemagne's wars had joined France, Germany and northern Italy under one rule and forced the Saxons into Christianity; his court at Aachen gathered scholars who revived Latin learning and copied the classical texts that survive today. His empire split among his grandsons, but the ideas of a Christian empire and of the Franks as heirs of Rome shaped medieval Europe.

events.title: The Book of Kells
events.summary: Monks of the Columban community, probably on Iona before Viking raids drove them to Kells in Ireland, produced a gospel book on calfskin whose decoration is as dense as metalwork: interlace, spirals and animals worked at a scale that needs magnification to follow, with pigments including imported lapis lazuli. It is the high point of insular art and evidence of how much learning and wealth Irish monasteries commanded. It has been at Trinity College Dublin since the seventeenth century.

events.title: The Ghana Empire controls the Sahel gold trade
events.summary: Between the Senegal and Niger rivers, the Soninke state that Arab geographers called Ghana taxed every load of gold going north and every load of salt coming south, and grew rich enough that al-Bakri described its king holding audience surrounded by gold-collared dogs. Its capital Koumbi Saleh had separate Muslim and royal quarters. Weakened by drought, Almoravid pressure and its own vassals, it was absorbed into the rising Mali Empire by about 1240. The modern republic took the name in 1957 in its honour.

events.title: The longship gives the Norse the sea and the rivers
events.summary: Clinker-built of overlapping oak planks riveted to a light frame, double-ended, steered by a side rudder and driven by one square sail or by oars, the longship was flexible enough to ride an Atlantic swell and shallow enough to row up a river and be dragged over a portage. The Gokstad and Oseberg ships, buried and recovered in Norway, show the craftsmanship. The design is what made three centuries of raiding, trading and settlement from Newfoundland to the Caspian physically possible.

events.title: Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire
events.summary: On the sacred hill of Mahendraparvata, north of the future Angkor, a prince returned from Java had a brahmin consecrate him as universal monarch, free of any foreign overlord, in the devaraja rite that bound the king to Shiva. The ceremony is known from an inscription carved more than two centuries later, so the detail is a court tradition rather than a record. Khmer chronology nevertheless begins here: the empire he started ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia for six hundred years.

events.title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and Al-Khwarizmi's algebra
events.summary: Under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and built on them. Around 820 Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise on solving equations whose title gave the world the word algebra and, in a second book, explained the Indian decimal numerals; a Latin corruption of his name gave us algorithm. Arabic became the language of science from Spain to Central Asia for four centuries.

events.title: The Treaty of Verdun splits Charlemagne's empire
events.summary: Three grandsons of Charlemagne ended three years of civil war by dividing the Carolingian empire into a western kingdom, an eastern kingdom and a long middle strip from the North Sea to Italy. Teams of commissioners surveyed revenues to make the shares equal. West Francia became France and East Francia became Germany; the unstable middle portion, Lotharingia, was fought over from Alsace to the Low Countries for the next eleven centuries. Few treaties have drawn a more durable line.

events.title: Gunpowder is invented in China
events.summary: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of immortality recorded a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burned violently in a Taoist text of about 850 CE. By 1044 the Song dynasty's military manual gave gunpowder recipes, and over the next two centuries the Chinese developed fire arrows, bombs, rockets, and the first true guns. Through the Mongols and the Islamic world, gunpowder reached Europe by the late thirteenth century, where cannon would end the age of castles.

events.title: The Danelaw divides England
events.summary: After Alfred of Wessex beat the Danish army at Edington, he and the Viking leader Guthrum agreed a frontier running roughly from London to Chester, north and east of which Danish law and custom applied. Scandinavian settlement left its mark on the land in thousands of place names ending in -by and -thorpe, in the word law itself, and in hundreds of everyday English words — sky, skin, egg, they. Wessex reconquered the territory in the tenth century, but the linguistic merger was permanent.

events.title: Austronesian sailors settle Madagascar
events.summary: Malagasy is an Austronesian language, closest to Ma'anyan of southeast Borneo, spoken on an island off Mozambique — the longest single displacement of any language family before the modern era, some eight thousand kilometres of open ocean and coastline. Genetic studies find both Indonesian and East African ancestry, and the settlers brought rice, bananas, taro and the outrigger canoe. When they arrived is contested: early traces appear by the first millennium, permanent villages from about the seventh to tenth centuries.

events.title: Chichén Itzá dominates the Maya north
events.summary: As the southern Maya cities empty, Chichén Itzá rises in northern Yucatán into the peninsula's dominant power — a cosmopolitan capital whose stepped pyramid of Kukulcán casts a serpent-shaped shadow at the equinoxes, and whose Great Ball Court is the largest in Mesoamerica. Its art mixes Maya and central-Mexican styles, evidence of trade and ideas moving across the Gulf. The city declines by around 1200, but its sacred cenote keeps drawing pilgrims until the Spanish conquest.

events.title: Yasovarman I founds the first city at Angkor
events.summary: Yasovarman I, who took the throne in 889, moved his capital to the plain north of the Tonle Sap and laid out a square city around the temple-mountain of Phnom Bakheng, with a reservoir seven kilometres long, the East Baray, fed by diverted rivers. He founded over a hundred hermitages across the kingdom and had identical inscriptions cut at each. Angkor stayed the Khmer capital for five centuries, and the hydraulic city built around these reservoirs supported one of the largest pre-industrial populations in the world.

events.title: Goryeo reunites Korea and gives it its name
events.summary: Wang Geon, a merchant's son turned general, took power in the confusion of Silla's collapse and by 936 held the whole peninsula, naming his state after the old northern kingdom of Goguryeo — the source, through Arab and Persian traders, of the western word Korea. Goryeo ran a civil service examination, made Seon Buddhism a state religion, produced celadon ceramics that Chinese connoisseurs ranked first in the world, and survived the Mongols as a tributary before falling to its own generals in 1392.

events.title: Córdoba and the brilliance of al-Andalus
events.summary: Under the Umayyad caliphate proclaimed in 929, Córdoba becomes western Europe's greatest city — paved, lamp-lit, with a vast library and the Great Mosque's forest of arches. Muslim, Jewish and Christian scholars work in overlapping worlds that produce Averroes's Aristotle commentaries and Maimonides's philosophy. Even after the caliphate fragments, translation schools in Toledo channel this learning north into Latin Europe.

events.title: Iceland founds the Althing assembly
events.summary: Norse settlers of Iceland, having no king, gather at Thingvellir in 930 to found the Althing: a general assembly where chieftains make law and judge disputes, with a Lawspeaker reciting the law aloud from the Law Rock. It is the oldest surviving parliament, and its most famous decision comes in 1000, when Iceland peacefully adopts Christianity by arbitration to avoid civil war. Suspended under Danish rule in 1800, the Althing was restored and continues as Iceland's legislature today.

events.title: Hywel Dda's law is codified in Wales
events.summary: Welsh tradition credits King Hywel the Good with summoning jurists to Whitland to sift and settle the law of his kingdoms. The texts that survive are later, but they preserve a distinct legal world: compensation rather than execution for most offences, land divided among all sons, and property and divorce rights for women well beyond what English common law then allowed. Welsh law remained in use alongside English rule until the Acts of Union of the 1530s abolished it.

events.title: Song China's economic and technological revolution
events.summary: Song China, from 960 to 1279, was the most advanced economy in the world: it issued the first paper money, produced iron on a scale Europe would not match for seven centuries, built ocean-going junks with watertight compartments, and its cities of Kaifeng and Hangzhou passed a million inhabitants. Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass and fossils; Su Song built an astronomical clock tower. Civil service examinations drew officials from a broad gentry. The Mongols conquered the Song in 1279.

events.title: Ani, the city of a thousand and one churches
events.summary: The Bagratid kings made Ani, on a ravine-protected plateau in what is now eastern Turkey, their capital in 961, and it grew to a walled city of perhaps a hundred thousand on the trade routes east. Its architects worked out ribbed vaulting and pointed arches in the cathedral of Trdat before either appeared in Gothic Europe. Byzantine annexation, a Seljuk sack and finally an earthquake and shifting trade emptied it, and it stands abandoned, a World Heritage site since 2016.

events.title: Otto I is crowned emperor and the Holy Roman Empire begins
events.summary: Otto the Great had ended the Magyar raids at the Lechfeld in 955 and bound the German duchies to his crown through bishops he appointed himself. In 962 the pope crowned him emperor in Rome, reviving the title Charlemagne had held and tying it permanently to the German kingship. The empire that resulted lasted until 1806, an elective federation of hundreds of principalities that Voltaire would mock as neither holy, Roman, nor an empire — and that nonetheless organised central Europe for eight centuries.

events.title: Harald Bluetooth raises the Jelling stones
events.summary: At Jelling in Jutland, King Harald set up a carved stone declaring that he had won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian, beside an earlier stone his father raised for his mother. One face carries the oldest depiction of Christ in Scandinavia, still wrapped in pagan interlace. Danes call the larger stone their country's birth certificate: it is the first use of the name Denmark inside the country itself. Harald's nickname was borrowed a thousand years later for a wireless standard.

events.title: Al-Azhar is founded in Cairo
events.summary: The Fatimid caliphs built a congregational mosque for their new capital and within two decades attached a teaching institution to it, endowed to pay scholars and house students. Saladin's Sunni conquest closed it for a time; it reopened and became the leading centre of Sunni legal and theological learning, which it remains. Its continuous teaching since the tenth century makes it, with Qarawiyyin in Fez, one of the oldest operating universities in the world.

events.title: Erik the Red settles Greenland
events.summary: Outlawed from Iceland for killings, Erik spent his exile exploring the fjords of a large land to the west, named it Greenland to attract settlers, and came back with a fleet. Two settlements of farmers ran sheep and cattle on the southwestern coast for nearly five centuries, exported walrus ivory to Europe, built stone churches and sent the voyages that reached North America. They died out or left in the fifteenth century, in a cooling climate and a collapsed ivory market.

events.title: Hugh Capet is elected king and founds a dynasty
events.summary: When the last Carolingian of the western kingdom died, the magnates chose the count of Paris instead of the dead king's uncle. Hugh controlled little more than the country between Paris and Orleans, but he had his son crowned in his own lifetime, and his descendants in the direct and collateral lines — Capetians, Valois, Bourbons — held the French throne until 1848 and still reign in Spain. The kingdom they slowly assembled around that small domain became France.

events.title: The Christianisation of Kievan Rus'
events.summary: In 988 Vladimir the Great, prince of Kiev, accepted baptism from Constantinople, married a Byzantine princess and had his people baptised in the Dnieper, choosing Orthodox Christianity over Islam, Judaism and Latin Christianity according to the Primary Chronicle's famous story. The decision bound the East Slavs to the Byzantine world, its Cyrillic script, church architecture and law. Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their religious and cultural origins to this event, and compete over its legacy.

events.title: Vladimir baptises Kievan Rus
events.summary: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev accepts Byzantine Christianity in 988, marries the emperor's sister, and has his people baptised in the Dnieper. With the faith come Church Slavonic writing, icon painting, masonry churches and Byzantine political ideas — the cultural foundation shared by Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. After Constantinople's fall, Moscow's churchmen will style their city the 'Third Rome', heir to that inheritance.

events.title: Camel caravans make the Sahara a highway
events.summary: The camel, introduced to North Africa in the first centuries CE, made it possible to cross twenty days of desert with a load, and by the eleventh century regular caravans linked the Sahel to the Mediterranean. West African gold went north in enough quantity to mint the coinage of Christian Europe and Islamic Egypt; salt, copper, books and horses came south, along with Islam, Arabic literacy and a large traffic in enslaved people. The routes made the Sahel empires possible and tied them into world commerce.

events.title: Norse voyages reach North America
events.summary: Around 1000, Leif Erikson's Greenlanders sail beyond to a land of meadows and wild grapes they call Vinland. The sagas' claim was long doubted until excavations at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland uncovered Norse turf halls, iron rivets and a bronze pin — the only confirmed pre-Columbian European site in the Americas. The settlements are brief; the two halves of humanity part again for five centuries.

events.title: Polynesians settle the remote Pacific
events.summary: Sailing double-hulled canoes and navigating by stars, swells, birds and cloud, Polynesian voyagers settled the islands of the eastern Pacific in a final burst between about 1000 and 1280 CE: the Society Islands, Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and, last, Aotearoa New Zealand. Radiocarbon dates have compressed this expansion to a few centuries, far later than once thought. It was the last great settlement of uninhabited land by humans and the most remarkable feat of pre-modern navigation.

events.title: The Swahili city-states of the East African coast
events.summary: From about 1000 CE, Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar, Sofala and other stone-built towns along the East African coast linked the interior's gold, ivory and slaves to the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean, with Arab, Persian, Indian and Chinese partners. Their people spoke Swahili, a Bantu language with Arabic loanwords, and were Muslim from the eleventh century. Kilwa minted its own coins and Ibn Battuta praised it in 1331. The Portuguese sacked the coast after 1505.

events.title: Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji
events.summary: At the Heian court, the lady-in-waiting known as Murasaki Shikibu composes a vast prose narrative of the shining prince Genji — psychological, ironic, and structured across generations. Written in Japanese kana while men wrote official Chinese, it is often called the world's first novel, and it fixes an aesthetic of impermanence and refined feeling that runs through Japanese art from ink painting to film.

events.title: Ferdowsi completes the Shahnameh
events.summary: Thirty years' work produced some fifty thousand rhyming couplets carrying Iran's kings and heroes from the creation to the Arab conquest — Rostam, Sohrab, Zahhak and the rest. Ferdowsi wrote in a deliberately Persian vocabulary at a time when Arabic dominated learned writing, and the poem is usually credited with keeping the language and its historical memory intact. It remains the national epic of Iran, recited and illustrated for a thousand years, and its manuscripts are among the great achievements of Persian painting.

events.title: The Chola empire projects Indian power across the seas
events.summary: From their Tamil heartland, Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra build south India's greatest empire: the towering Brihadisvara temple, a formidable navy, and expeditions that reach the Ganges, Sri Lanka and — uniquely in Indian history — the Srivijaya ports of Sumatra and Malaya. Chola bronze sculpture, above all the dancing Shiva Nataraja, becomes one of the world's great artistic traditions.

events.title: Brian Boru falls at Clontarf
events.summary: Brian Boru, the one man to make himself high king of most of Ireland, fought a coalition of the Leinster Irish and the Norse of Dublin and Orkney outside Dublin on Good Friday and won, but was killed in his tent as the battle ended. Later tradition turned it into a national victory over the Vikings, which it was not — Norse and Irish fought on both sides — but it broke the power of Dublin and left Ireland's high kingship contested until the Normans arrived.

events.title: Ibn al-Haytham founds the science of optics
events.summary: Working in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) completed his Book of Optics around 1021, showing by experiment that vision occurs when light reflected from objects enters the eye, refuting the ancient theory of rays emitted by the eye, and describing the camera obscura, refraction and the anatomy of the eye. His insistence on testing hypotheses by controlled experiment has earned him a claim to be the first modern scientist. Translated into Latin, his work influenced Kepler and the development of lenses.

events.title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
events.summary: Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna, born near Bukhara, completed his Canon of Medicine in 1025, a five-volume synthesis of Greek, Persian and Indian medicine organised systematically, with sections on anatomy, diseases, drugs and the testing of remedies. Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, it was a standard medical textbook in European universities into the seventeenth century and in the Islamic world longer. His philosophical works were equally influential on scholastic thought.

events.title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
events.summary: Between 1039 and 1048 the artisan Bi Sheng made individual characters of baked clay, set them in a frame with wax and resin, printed, and then reused them, as the polymath Shen Kuo recorded in his Dream Pool Essays. Woodblock printing, older and better suited to thousands of Chinese characters, remained dominant in China, but movable type was developed further in Korea, where the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type, seven decades before Gutenberg.

events.title: The magnetic compass is used for navigation
events.summary: Chinese texts of the eleventh century describe magnetised needles floating in water to indicate south, first for geomancy, and Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks of 1117 records their use by ship pilots at sea, the earliest clear evidence of navigation by compass. Within a century the instrument appears in Arabic and European sources, probably transmitted along the maritime routes of the Indian Ocean. Together with the sternpost rudder and watertight bulkheads, also Chinese, it made long ocean voyages routine.

events.title: Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico
events.summary: Around 1050 CE a settlement near present-day St. Louis grew rapidly into Cahokia, a planned city of perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people with more than a hundred earthen mounds, the largest, Monks Mound, covering as much ground as the Great Pyramid. Its Mississippian culture, based on maize, spread its art and religion across the eastern United States. The city was abandoned by about 1350, for reasons that may include floods, drought and political breakdown, and its builders' name is unknown.

events.title: The West Baray: Angkor's engineered water
events.summary: Eight kilometres by two, held by earth embankments above the surrounding plain rather than dug into it, the West Baray is the largest of the Angkorian reservoirs and still holds water. It was begun in the eleventh century under Suryavarman I and finished by his successor. Airborne laser survey has since mapped the canals, dykes and field systems around it and shown Angkor to have been a low-density urban sprawl of roughly a thousand square kilometres. Whether the barays were primarily religious or agricultural is still argued.

events.title: The East–West Schism splits Christendom
events.summary: In 1054 papal legates lay a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicates them back — the symbolic break between Latin West and Greek East after centuries of drift over papal authority, the filioque clause and ritual. The split hardens irreversibly when the Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople in 1204. Catholic and Orthodox Christianity develop separately from then on; the mutual excommunications were lifted only in 1965, the division itself never healed.

events.title: Stamford Bridge ends the Viking age in England
events.summary: Harald Hardrada of Norway, the last great Viking warlord, invaded Yorkshire to claim the English throne. Harold Godwinson marched his army two hundred miles north in four days, caught the Norwegians unarmoured at a river crossing and destroyed them; of some three hundred ships, two dozen were needed to carry the survivors home. Three weeks later Harold marched back south and lost to William at Hastings. Large-scale Scandinavian invasion of England was over.

events.title: The Norman conquest of England
events.summary: William of Normandy landed in Sussex, killed Harold Godwinson at Hastings and had himself crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day. Within twenty years the English landholding class had been replaced almost entirely, castles stood over every town, and the Domesday Book of 1086 recorded who held what down to the last plough team — the most detailed survey any European state attempted for centuries. French became the language of law and rule, and the collision of it with English produced the vocabulary the language still has.

events.title: Manzikert opens Anatolia to the Turks
events.summary: The emperor Romanos IV met the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan near Lake Van and was beaten and captured, partly because a rival faction withdrew its troops during the battle. The defeat itself was not catastrophic; the civil war that followed was, and within a decade Turkish groups had settled across the Anatolian plateau that had supplied Byzantium with most of its soldiers and taxes. The appeal for western help that followed helped produce the First Crusade.

events.title: The Investiture Controversy and the walk to Canossa
events.summary: Emperor Henry IV, excommunicated for insisting on appointing bishops, stands three days barefoot in the snow at Canossa in 1077 to beg Pope Gregory VII's absolution. The struggle over investiture ends in the Concordat of Worms compromise of 1122, but its deeper legacy is the idea that spiritual and secular power are distinct and can check one another — a peculiarly European separation with a long constitutional future.

events.title: The first universities
events.summary: The University of Bologna, traditionally dated to 1088, was the first institution to grant degrees recognised beyond its own city; Paris and Oxford followed within a century. Older centres of higher learning existed elsewhere, notably al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, and al-Azhar in Cairo, and Buddhist Nalanda in India. The European university's distinctive features, self-governing guilds of masters and students and formal degrees, spread with colonialism to become the worldwide model.

events.title: The First Crusade
events.summary: Answering Pope Urban II's call at Clermont in 1095, tens of thousands of western Europeans marched east, massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way, and in July 1099 stormed Jerusalem, slaughtering much of its Muslim and Jewish population. They founded crusader states that lasted until 1291. Eight more major crusades followed over two centuries, embittering relations between Christians and Muslims, and between Latin and Greek Christians after the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

events.title: Great Zimbabwe is built
events.summary: From about 1100 CE the Shona built Great Zimbabwe, a city of dry-stone walls, the largest of which, the Great Enclosure, stands eleven metres high with a perimeter of 250 metres, laid without mortar. The city of perhaps 18,000 people controlled gold and ivory trade to the Swahili coast; Chinese porcelain and Persian glass have been found there. Colonial-era writers denied its African origin; archaeology has long established it. It was abandoned around 1450 as trade routes shifted.

events.title: Angkor Wat is built by the Khmer Empire
events.summary: King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat in present-day Cambodia in the first half of the twelfth century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, the largest religious monument in the world by land area. Its five towers represent Mount Meru; its galleries carry over a kilometre of bas-reliefs. Angkor, the surrounding city, fed by a vast irrigation network, may have held nearly a million people. The temple later became Buddhist and has never been abandoned.

events.title: Portugal becomes a kingdom
events.summary: Afonso Henriques, count of a frontier province of León, defeated his own mother's forces in 1128 and at Zamora in 1143 had his royal title acknowledged by his cousin the king of León; the papacy confirmed it in 1179. Four years after Zamora he took Lisbon from the Muslims with the help of a passing crusader fleet. The borders settled in the thirteenth century have barely moved since, which makes Portugal one of the oldest states in Europe inside its present frontiers.

events.title: Abbot Suger invents Gothic architecture at Saint-Denis
events.summary: Rebuilding the royal abbey north of Paris, Suger's masons combined the pointed arch, the rib vault and the flying buttress so that the walls no longer carried the roof and could be opened up into stained glass. Suger wrote that the light was a way of approaching God; the engineering was what let him have it. The new choir, consecrated in 1144, was copied at Chartres, Notre-Dame, Reims and Amiens, and the style spread across Europe for four hundred years.

events.title: Maimonides codifies Jewish law and argues with Aristotle
events.summary: Born in Córdoba, driven out by the Almohads and settled in Cairo as physician to Saladin's court, Moses ben Maimon wrote the Mishneh Torah, the first complete systematic code of Jewish law, in clear Hebrew anyone literate could follow. He then wrote the Guide for the Perplexed in Arabic, reconciling scripture with Aristotelian philosophy. Both were fiercely contested in his own century and became foundational afterwards; Aquinas and Spinoza both read him closely.

events.title: Jayavarman VII rebuilds Angkor as a Buddhist capital
events.summary: After driving out a Cham invasion that had sacked the capital, Jayavarman VII built on a scale nobody matched: the walled city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon and its towers of serene faces at the centre, the monasteries of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, and, his inscriptions claim, a hundred and two hospitals and over a hundred rest houses along the royal roads. He was a Mahayana Buddhist, and the shift from Shiva to the compassionate bodhisattva is written into the stone.

events.title: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia
events.summary: Armenians displaced from their highlands by the Seljuks built a new state on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, which Leo II raised to a kingdom in 1198. It allied with the crusader states and later the Mongols, traded through Ayas with Genoa and Venice, produced the finest Armenian illuminated manuscripts and a code of law under Smbat, and adopted a good deal of Frankish court culture. Mamluk invasions ended it in 1375; its last king died in Paris.

events.title: The Dresden Codex, a surviving Maya book
events.summary: Four Maya books escaped the Spanish burnings, and the best of them is a screenfold of bark paper coated in lime plaster, thirty-nine leaves painted on both sides. It contains an almanac, ritual tables, and a Venus table that tracks the planet's 584-day cycle with corrections accurate to a few hours over centuries, plus eclipse predictions. Sold to the Saxon royal library in 1739, it was the key text for cracking Maya numbers and calendar in the nineteenth century.

events.title: The Inca begin as one valley kingdom among many
events.summary: Before the empire there was a small polity in the Cusco basin, one competitor among several in the southern Andes, whose founding is told in the legend of Manco Capac emerging from Lake Titicaca with a golden staff. For two centuries it fought neighbours over a valley. The turn came around 1438, when the Chanka attacked Cusco and a prince who took the name Pachacuti beat them, deposed his father and began the conquests that made Tawantinsuyu. The early chronology rests on oral tradition recorded after the conquest.

events.title: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
events.summary: Under the Zagwe king Lalibela, masons cut eleven churches downward out of solid volcanic rock in the Ethiopian highlands, freeing each building from the hillside and then hollowing it out, roof first. Bet Giyorgis, a cross in plan sunk in its own pit, is the most famous. The complex was conceived as a new Jerusalem after Muslim control of the Holy Land cut off pilgrimage, and it is still in continuous use by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church eight centuries later.

events.title: The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
events.summary: A crusade aimed at Egypt was diverted by debts to Venice and a Byzantine succession dispute into attacking the greatest Christian city in the world. For three days in April 1204 the crusaders looted churches, burned quarters of the city and carried off relics and the bronze horses now in Venice. A Latin empire was installed for fifty-seven years. Byzantium recovered the city in 1261 but never its strength, and the schism between the Greek and Latin churches hardened into permanent enmity.

events.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol conquests
events.summary: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and led them against northern China, Central Asia and Persia; his successors reached Kyiv, Baghdad, which they sacked in 1258, and all of China, completed by Kublai Khan in 1279. The largest contiguous land empire in history killed millions but then secured the trade routes across Eurasia, moving merchants, missionaries, paper money, printing and, in the fourteenth century, the plague. It fragmented into four khanates within a century.

events.title: Las Navas de Tolosa breaks Almohad power in Iberia
events.summary: The kings of Castile, Aragon and Navarre, with Portuguese and transpyrenean contingents and a papal crusade indulgence, combined against the Almohad caliph in the Sierra Morena and destroyed his army. The victory opened Andalusia: Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248, and Muslim rule in Iberia shrank to the emirate of Granada for its last two and a half centuries. The battle is the hinge of the Reconquista and still marked in Spain as a national date.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.summary: At Runnymede in June 1215 rebellious barons forced King John of England to seal a charter limiting royal power: no free man was to be imprisoned or dispossessed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, and taxes required consent. It was annulled within months and reissued in revised form after John's death. Most of its clauses were feudal and specific, but its principle that the ruler is under the law became a touchstone for later constitutions.

events.title: The Mongols destroy the Khwarazmian Empire
events.summary: A Khwarazmian governor seized a Mongol trade caravan and executed its merchants, and the shah then killed Genghis Khan's envoys. The retaliation erased the richest Muslim state in Central Asia in two years: Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Nishapur and Urgench were stormed, their craftsmen deported and much of the rest killed, and the irrigation works of Khurasan wrecked. Contemporary death tolls are surely exaggerated but the destruction was real, and it opened the road into Persia and Europe.

events.title: Snorri Sturluson writes down the Norse myths
events.summary: An Icelandic chieftain, lawspeaker and politician compiled a handbook for poets that explains the kennings of skaldic verse — and to explain them has to retell the myths behind them. Odin, Thor, Loki, the world tree and Ragnarok survive in narrative form largely because Snorri, a Christian writing two centuries after conversion, set them down. With the older Poetic Edda and the Icelandic sagas it is the foundation of almost everything later readers know about Norse mythology.

events.title: Goryeo Korea casts the world's first metal movable type
events.summary: Korean printers under the Goryeo dynasty cast movable type in bronze generations before Gutenberg; the Buddhist anthology Jikji, printed in 1377 and now in Paris, is the oldest surviving book made with metal movable type. The same era carves the Tripitaka Koreana — over eighty thousand flawless woodblocks of the Buddhist canon, still preserved at Haeinsa temple — as an act of national devotion against the Mongol invasions.

events.title: The yam relay carries messages across Eurasia
events.summary: Ogedei organised a network of staging posts a day's ride apart across the empire, each obliged to keep horses, food and shelter ready. A courier carrying the paiza tablet could change mounts and ride on, covering several hundred kilometres a day; Marco Polo claimed ten thousand stations. The system was a tax on the communities that maintained it, but it let one government hold together an empire from Korea to Hungary, and it moved merchants, envoys and news as well as orders.

events.title: Sundiata Keita founds the Mali Empire
events.summary: At the battle of Kirina around 1235, Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso king Sumanguru and unites the Mande peoples into the Mali Empire, soon the master of the West African gold trade. The Epic of Sundiata, sung by griots for eight centuries, preserves his story — the crippled prince who rose to found an empire — and tradition links his assembly to the Kouroukan Fouga charter of laws. His successors, including Mansa Musa, make Mali a byword for wealth.

events.title: The Secret History of the Mongols is written
events.summary: The oldest surviving work of Mongolian literature is a family chronicle of Genghis Khan written for the ruling house shortly after his death — his childhood in poverty, the murder of his half-brother, his wife's abduction, the betrayals and alliances, in verse and dialogue as much as narrative. It survives only in a Chinese transcription made to teach the language, the Mongolian original being lost. It is the single indispensable source for the empire's own account of itself.

events.title: The Golden Horde rules the Russian principalities
events.summary: Batu's campaign of 1237 to 1241 burned Ryazan, Vladimir and Kiev and reached Hungary and the Adriatic before turning back on the great khan's death. The khanate he left on the lower Volga took census and tribute from the Russian princes for two centuries, issuing them patents to rule and playing them against each other, while itself turning Turkic in speech and Muslim in religion. Moscow rose as its tax collector, then outgrew it; the khanate splintered into the Crimean, Kazan and Astrakhan states.

events.title: The Pax Mongolica links Eurasia end to end
events.summary: For a century Mongol rule makes the Silk Road safer than it has ever been: merchants like the Polos travel from Venice to Khubilai's Beijing, missionaries and envoys cross the continent, and Chinese techniques — printing, gunpowder, playing cards — drift west. The same connectivity carries catastrophe: the Black Death rides the trade routes to the Crimea and thence into Europe, killing perhaps a third of its people.

events.title: The moai of Rapa Nui
events.summary: On Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the most isolated inhabited place on Earth, Polynesian settlers carved nearly a thousand monolithic figures from volcanic tuff between about 1250 and 1500 and moved statues weighing up to 80 tonnes kilometres from the quarry, most likely by 'walking' them upright with ropes, as experiments have shown. The old story of ecological suicide through deforestation has been challenged; disease and slave raids after European contact in 1722 did the greatest damage to the population.

events.title: Hulagu sacks Baghdad and ends the Abbasid caliphate
events.summary: Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu brought siege engineers and Chinese catapults to the Abbasid capital, broke its walls in under two weeks and sacked it for a week more. The last caliph was killed, reportedly rolled in a carpet and trampled so that no royal blood touched the ground. The House of Wisdom's libraries were destroyed. Five centuries of Abbasid caliphate ended, and the shock is still cited in the Muslim world as the end of a golden age, though scholarship continued elsewhere.

events.title: Ain Jalut stops the Mongol advance
events.summary: In the Jezreel valley in Galilee, a Mamluk army from Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars drew a Mongol force into a feigned-retreat trap of its own kind and destroyed it. Hulagu had withdrawn most of his troops east after the great khan's death, so the defeated army was a detachment rather than the full horde — but it was the first significant Mongol defeat in open battle, and the frontier settled at the Euphrates. Egypt and the Mamluk state were never conquered.

events.title: The Solomonic dynasty claims descent from Solomon and Sheba
events.summary: Yekuno Amlak displaced the Zagwe kings and founded a line that ruled Ethiopia, with interruptions, until Haile Selassie was deposed in 1974. Its legitimacy rested on the Kebra Nagast's account of the Queen of Sheba's son by Solomon bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum, a claim written into the imperial title and eventually into the 1955 constitution. Few dynasties anywhere have used a single founding story for seven hundred years of continuous political argument.

events.title: Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan dynasty
events.summary: Kublai took a Chinese dynastic name, built a capital at Dadu — now Beijing — and by 1279 had finished off the Southern Song, making him the first non-Chinese ruler of the whole country. The Yuan ranked its subjects by origin with Chinese at the bottom, issued paper money across the empire, extended the Grand Canal to the new capital and employed foreigners like Marco Polo. Inflation, floods and rebellion brought it down in under a century, and the Ming drove the court back to the steppe.

events.title: Typhoons wreck the Mongol invasions of Japan
events.summary: Kublai Khan sent two fleets against Kyushu, the second among the largest naval expeditions attempted before the twentieth century. Samurai defence and a stone wall around Hakata Bay held the beachheads, and storms then destroyed both fleets at anchor. The Japanese called the winds kamikaze, divine wind, a phrase revived for the suicide pilots of 1944. Victory brought no plunder to pay the defenders, and the resulting resentment helped bring down the Kamakura shogunate.

events.title: Majapahit dominates the Indonesian archipelago
events.summary: Founded in eastern Java out of the wreckage of a Mongol invasion it had first invited and then turned on, Majapahit under the minister Gajah Mada claimed authority over ports from Sumatra to New Guinea. The court poem Nagarakretagama lists its dependencies and describes a capital at Trowulan of brick and water gardens. Hindu-Buddhist in religion and commercial in method, it faded as Islam spread through the coastal trading towns; the conventional end date of 1527 is disputed, with some historians ending it in 1478.

events.title: Zhou Daguan describes Angkor from the inside
events.summary: A Chinese envoy of the Yuan court spent eleven months at Angkor and wrote up what he saw: the gilded towers, the king's processions, the slaves and the tax system, houses, clothing, childbirth, the three-crop rice year and the crocodiles in the moat. It is the only eyewitness account of the Khmer Empire by anyone who was there, and since the Khmer themselves left inscriptions but no narrative history, almost everything known about daily life at Angkor comes from this one short book.

events.title: Osman founds the dynasty that becomes an empire
events.summary: On the Byzantine frontier in northwestern Anatolia, one of many small Turkish warrior principalities began expanding under a chief named Osman, whose followers were called Osmanli — Ottomans. Its advantage was position: it faced a weakening Byzantium and could absorb fighters and converts from both sides. His son took Bursa in 1326 and the dynasty crossed into Europe within a generation. The 1299 date is a later convention; the earliest Ottoman written sources are a century and a half after the fact.

events.title: Djenné builds the world's largest mud-brick building
events.summary: On the Niger floodplain in Mali, the trading town of Djenné built a congregational mosque of sun-dried earth brick rendered in mud plaster, with projecting palm-wood beams that double as permanent scaffolding. The present structure dates from 1907 but follows the plan of a thirteenth or fourteenth-century original. The whole town replasters it by hand every year in a festival, which is what keeps a mud building of that size standing in a monsoon climate. It is the best-known example of Sudano-Sahelian architecture.

events.title: Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa
events.summary: The last large habitable landmass on Earth to be reached by people was settled from eastern Polynesia around 1300, a date now pinned tightly by radiocarbon dating of rat-gnawed seeds and by the rat's own arrival. The settlers met a cold, large country with no mammals and hunted the flightless moa to extinction within two centuries, then reorganised around fortified pa, kumara cultivation and iwi descent groups, becoming Maori — a distinct culture built on Polynesian foundations in a temperate land.

events.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage displays Mali's golden wealth
events.summary: The emperor of Mali crosses Africa to Mecca with a caravan of thousands, spending and giving away so much gold that Cairo's price of bullion reportedly sags for years. The spectacle puts Mali on European maps — literally, crowned and holding a nugget in the Catalan Atlas — and advertises the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt on which Timbuktu and Djenné grow rich.

events.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage from Mali
events.summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, travelled to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan of thousands and so much gold that its price in Cairo reportedly fell for years. The journey advertised West Africa's wealth to the Islamic world and to Europe, where Mali soon appeared on the Catalan Atlas. Musa returned with scholars and architects, and Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning whose manuscripts survive today.

events.title: Ibn Battuta's travels
events.summary: Leaving Tangier on pilgrimage in 1325, the Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta travelled for nearly thirty years through North and East Africa, Arabia, Persia, Central Asia, India, where he served as a judge in Delhi, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and, he claimed, China, then across the Sahara to Mali. His Rihla, dictated on his return, is the fullest picture of the fourteenth-century Islamic world, though some passages are borrowed and some journeys doubted.

events.title: Tenochtitlan: the Aztec capital on the lake
events.summary: On an island in Lake Texcoco — where, tradition says, an eagle perched on a cactus marked the spot — the Mexica found Tenochtitlan in 1325. Two centuries later it is one of the world's largest cities: canals, causeways, aqueducts, floating chinampa gardens feeding perhaps two hundred thousand people, and the Templo Mayor at its heart. The eagle and cactus now sit on Mexico's flag.

events.title: Vijayanagara, the great city of southern India
events.summary: Founded in 1336, the Vijayanagara Empire ruled most of southern India for two centuries from a capital at Hampi that Portuguese and Persian visitors described as among the largest and richest cities in the world, with markets of gems and horses and temples whose towers still stand. Its kings patronised Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit literature and Carnatic music. A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated the empire at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the city.

events.title: The Hundred Years' War
events.summary: English kings claiming the French crown and holding land in Aquitaine fought the Valois for one hundred and sixteen years, in bursts separated by truces and plague. Longbowmen destroyed French chivalry at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt; gunpowder artillery ended English resistance at Castillon. When it stopped, England held only Calais, France had a standing army and permanent taxation to pay for it, and both countries had acquired something recognisable as national feeling rather than dynastic loyalty.

events.title: The Black Death
events.summary: Bubonic plague, carried along Mongol trade routes from Central Asia, reached the Crimea in 1346 and spread by ship through the Mediterranean and across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population and comparable shares elsewhere, the deadliest pandemic in recorded history. Labour shortages raised wages and loosened serfdom; persecutions of Jews and flagellant movements followed. Plague recurred in waves for four centuries.

events.title: Chinampas feed the valley of Mexico
events.summary: In the shallow lakes around Tenochtitlan, farmers staked out rectangular plots, built them up with mud dredged from the lake bed and vegetation, and anchored the edges with willows. The beds sit just above the water and wick it up continuously, so they never need irrigating and can carry several crops a year. Yields were high enough to feed one of the largest cities on Earth. Chinampas are still worked at Xochimilco and are recognised by the UN as a globally important agricultural system.

events.title: The Golden Bull fixes the Holy Roman constitution
events.summary: Emperor Charles IV's Golden Bull settles how Holy Roman emperors are made: seven named prince-electors choose the king of the Romans by majority, with elaborate ceremonial and no papal confirmation required. By entrenching the electors' privileges it fixes the empire as a decentralised federation of princes rather than a monarchy — a constitutional arrangement that endures, remarkably, until Napoleon dissolves the empire in 1806.

events.title: Timur builds the last great steppe empire
events.summary: A Turco-Mongol emir from near Samarkand who married into the Chinggisid line and ruled through puppet khans, Timur campaigned for thirty-five years from Delhi to Ankara and Damascus, leaving towers of skulls and deported craftsmen behind him. The craftsmen built Samarkand: the Gur-e-Amir, the Registan and the Bibi-Khanym mosque. He died marching on Ming China. His descendant Babur founded the Mughal empire in India, and Timurid astronomy under Ulugh Beg produced the best star catalogue before the telescope.

events.title: Ibn Khaldun writes the Muqaddimah
events.summary: Sheltering in a castle in what is now Algeria, a Tunisian jurist and diplomat wrote an introduction to universal history that turned into something new: an attempt to explain why states rise and fall. Ibn Khaldun argued from asabiyyah, group solidarity, which is strong among hard desert peoples, wins them cities, and decays over three or four generations of comfort until the next group arrives. He also analysed taxation, labour and the effects of climate. Later readers called it the first work of sociology.

events.title: Kulikovo: Moscow beats the Golden Horde in the field
events.summary: Dmitry of Moscow, blessed beforehand by the monk Sergius of Radonezh, gathered the northern Russian princes and defeated the Horde commander Mamai on the upper Don, winning the name Donskoy. Tokhtamysh sacked Moscow two years later and tribute went on for another century, so the battle changed less than the chronicles claim. What it did establish was that the Horde could be beaten and that Moscow, not Tver or Novgorod, would lead the effort — the beginning of a Russian state.

events.title: The Battle of Kosovo
events.summary: A Serbian-led coalition met Sultan Murad I on the field of blackbirds and both commanders died — Murad stabbed in his tent by a Serbian noble, Prince Lazar captured and executed. The battle itself was close to a draw and probably a tactical Ottoman success; Serbia became a vassal and was annexed seventy years later. Its afterlife mattered far more than its outcome: the Kosovo cycle of epic poetry made the defeat the central myth of Serbian nationhood, invoked repeatedly into the 1990s.

events.title: Yi Seong-gye founds Joseon
events.summary: A general ordered to invade Ming China turned his army around instead, took the throne and moved the capital to Hanyang, now Seoul. Joseon replaced Buddhism with Neo-Confucianism as the organising doctrine of the state, recruited officials by examination from a hereditary yangban class, and kept meticulous annals for five centuries — the Veritable Records run to nearly two thousand volumes. It was one of the longest unbroken dynasties in world history, ending only with Japanese annexation in 1910.

events.title: The Italian Renaissance
events.summary: In fifteenth-century Florence, Venice and Rome, wealth from banking and trade paid for a revival of classical learning and a new art: Brunelleschi's dome and linear perspective, Donatello's and Michelangelo's sculpture, Leonardo's notebooks, Botticelli's and Raphael's painting, and Machiavelli's politics. Humanist scholars recovered Greek and Roman texts, many via Byzantine and Arabic transmission, and printing spread them. The Renaissance's celebration of human capacity, and its return to ancient sources, reshaped European thought.

events.title: The quipu: an empire administered on knotted cord
events.summary: The Inca ran a state of ten million people without writing as it is usually defined, using bundles of dyed cotton or wool cords whose knots, positions, colours and ply recorded numbers in base ten: census figures, tribute, herd counts, storehouse contents. Specialist khipukamayuq kept and read them. Roughly a thousand survive. Whether some also encoded narrative or language rather than numbers is an open research question, and a few recent studies argue they did.

events.title: Zheng He's treasure fleets
events.summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven expeditions of up to hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men through Southeast Asia to India, Hormuz, Arabia and the East African coast, exchanging gifts, collecting tribute and bringing back a giraffe for the emperor. The largest ships were far bigger than any European vessel of the time, though their exact size is disputed. The voyages ended when the court turned inward, decades before Portuguese ships entered the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Portugal takes Ceuta and begins overseas expansion
events.summary: A fleet under King John I and his sons stormed the Moroccan port of Ceuta in a single day, giving Portugal a foothold on the African side of the strait and a close look at the Saharan gold trade it stood at the end of. One of those sons, Henry the Navigator, spent the next forty years sponsoring voyages down the Atlantic coast, pushing past Cape Bojador in 1434. Historians conventionally date the European age of overseas empire from this raid.

events.title: The Aztec Triple Alliance is forged
events.summary: In 1428 Tenochtitlan joins Texcoco and Tlacopan to overthrow the Tepanec overlords of the Valley of Mexico, founding the Triple Alliance that becomes the Aztec Empire. Under rulers like Moctezuma I, alliance armies push tribute networks to both coasts, feeding Tenochtitlan's markets and temples with cloth, cacao, jade and captives for sacrifice. Within a century the alliance rules perhaps five million people — the empire whose wealth and rivalries Cortés will exploit when he lands in 1519.

events.title: Joan of Arc turns the Hundred Years’ War
events.summary: A seventeen-year-old peasant girl claiming saintly voices persuades the French court to give her an army, breaks the English siege of Orléans in nine days, and stands beside Charles VII at his coronation in Reims — reversing the momentum of the Hundred Years' War. Captured and sold to the English, Joan is burned as a heretic at Rouen in 1431, aged nineteen. A church court annuls the verdict in 1456; France expels the English by 1453.

events.title: Angkor falls to Ayutthaya
events.summary: In 1431 the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya sacks Angkor, and the Khmer court soon abandons the vast temple-city for Phnom Penh, closer to the sea trade. The move ends the empire that had engineered Southeast Asia's greatest hydraulic city — recent surveys show droughts and floods had already been breaking its canal network. Angkor Wat itself is never wholly deserted: Buddhist monks keep it alive as a shrine, and it remains the largest religious monument on Earth.

events.title: Nezahualcoyotl, the engineer-poet of Texcoco
events.summary: The ruler of Texcoco, second city of the Triple Alliance, built a sixteen-kilometre dyke across Lake Texcoco to keep brackish water off the chinampas and an aqueduct to supply Tenochtitlan with fresh water, and laid out botanical gardens at Texcotzingo. He is also the best attested poet of pre-conquest Mexico; verses attributed to him on the brevity of life are still taught in Mexican schools, and he is on the hundred-peso note. He is said to have promoted a single unnamed god.

events.title: The Inca Empire at its height
events.summary: From 1438 under Pachacuti the Inca expanded from Cusco to rule about twelve million people along 4,000 kilometres of the Andes, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas. Without writing, wheels or iron, they administered it with quipu knot records, a 40,000-kilometre road system with relay runners, storehouses, terraced farming and labour tax, and built Machu Picchu. A civil war and smallpox, arriving ahead of the Spaniards, weakened the empire before Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa in 1532.

events.title: The Kingdom of Benin and its bronzes
events.summary: From the reign of Oba Ewuare around 1440, the Edo kingdom of Benin, in present-day southern Nigeria, built a walled capital whose earthworks were among the largest in the world and produced brass plaques and heads by lost-wax casting of a refinement that astonished Europe. Portuguese visitors traded with it from the 1480s. A British punitive expedition burned Benin City in 1897 and looted thousands of artworks, whose return from Western museums is the subject of continuing negotiation.

events.title: King Sejong creates the Hangul alphabet
events.summary: King Sejong of Joseon Korea devised Hangul, a featural alphabet whose letter shapes mirror the positions of the mouth and tongue, and promulgated it in 1446 in the Hunminjeongeum, explaining that the Chinese characters used by the elite were too hard for common people. The literati resisted it for centuries and it became Korea's official script only in the modern era. Linguists regard it as one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created.

events.title: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press
events.summary: Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a screw press into a practical system around 1450, printing his Bible by 1455. Movable type had been used in China since the eleventh century and in Korea, where metal type printed the Jikji in 1377, but Gutenberg's process suited the small alphabet of Latin script and spread rapidly. Within fifty years European presses had printed millions of volumes, transforming scholarship, religion and politics.

events.title: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy and its Great Law
events.summary: The Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca nations united under the Great Law of Peace, attributed to the Peacemaker and Hiawatha; oral tradition and an eclipse mentioned in the founding story date it anywhere from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, so the date here is a placeholder within that range. The confederacy's council of chiefs, chosen by clan mothers, kept peace among its members for centuries and is cited, controversially, as an influence on American federalism.
