events.title: The Inca build Machu Picchu
events.summary: Around 1450 the Inca emperor Pachacuti orders a royal estate built on a ridge above the Urubamba gorge: Machu Picchu, some two hundred structures of mortarless stone fitted so precisely that a knife blade cannot enter the joints, watered by spring-fed fountains and terraced into the mountainside. Abandoned within a century amid the Spanish conquest, it was never found by the Spaniards. Hiram Bingham's 1911 expedition made it world-famous, and it stands as the most complete surviving Inca city.

events.title: The Qhapaq Nan road system
events.summary: Some forty thousand kilometres of road tied Tawantinsuyu together from southern Colombia to central Chile, paved and stepped where it climbed, carried over gorges on suspension bridges of woven grass rebuilt each year by the communities beneath them. Way stations and storehouses stood a day's travel apart, and relay runners, the chasqui, could carry a message or fresh fish from the coast to Cusco in days. The network was built without wheels, iron or draught animals.

events.title: The mit'a: taxation paid in work
events.summary: Inca subjects owed the state labour rather than money or goods: a rotating obligation to farm state and temple land, build roads, serve in the army or weave cloth, in return for which the state fed them while they worked and kept filled storehouses against famine. Village lands and community reciprocity stayed intact underneath it. The Spanish kept the name and broke the bargain, drafting whole provinces into the silver mines at Potosi and the mercury pits of Huancavelica, from which many never returned.

events.title: The Ottomans take Constantinople
events.summary: On 29 May 1453 the army of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, using enormous bronze cannon, breached the walls of Constantinople and ended the Eastern Roman Empire after eleven centuries. The city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul, and the empire went on to rule the Balkans, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt and North Africa for four centuries. Greek scholars fleeing west carried manuscripts that fed the Renaissance, and the closing of overland routes gave Europeans a reason to seek the sea route to Asia.

events.title: The Ottoman millet system institutionalises pluralism
events.summary: After taking Constantinople, Mehmed II confirms the Greek patriarch, the Armenian patriarch and the chief rabbi as heads of self-governing religious communities — the arrangement later formalised as the millet system. Each community runs its own courts, schools and charities under its clergy, in exchange for taxes and loyalty. It is not equality, but it lets an empire of dozens of faiths and languages function for centuries.

events.title: The Onin War opens a century of civil war
events.summary: A succession dispute inside the Ashikaga shogunate turned into ten years of fighting between rival coalitions in the streets of Kyoto itself, which was burned out and depopulated. Central authority effectively ceased: provincial deputies stopped obeying, retainers overthrew their lords, and Japan entered the Sengoku period of independent warlord domains that lasted until Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu reunified it. The cultural refugees who fled Kyoto carried the capital's arts into the provinces.

events.title: Timbuktu under the Songhai Empire
events.summary: Sunni Ali took Timbuktu in 1468 and built the Songhai Empire along the Niger, which under Askia Muhammad from 1493 became the largest state in West African history. Its cities of Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao hosted scholars, courts and markets in gold, salt and books; the Sankore mosque and private libraries held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine, many still surviving. A Moroccan army with firearms destroyed the empire at Tondibi in 1591.

events.title: The Spanish Inquisition is established
events.summary: Ferdinand and Isabella obtained a papal bull for a tribunal under royal rather than papal control, to investigate whether Jews and Muslims converted under pressure were practising in secret. It used denunciation, secret procedure and torture, held public sentencing ceremonies, and operated in Spain's American and Italian territories too. Estimates of those executed over three and a half centuries run to a few thousand, far below the propaganda figures of Spain's enemies, but its censorship and suspicion marked Spanish intellectual life deeply. It was abolished in 1834.

events.title: The Aztec sun stone is carved
events.summary: A basalt disc more than three metres across and weighing some twenty-four tonnes, carved with a central face ringed by the signs of the four previous world ages and the twenty day names of the ritual calendar. It is a cosmological statement rather than a working calendar or clock. Buried after the conquest and dug up in Mexico City's main square in 1790, it now anchors the National Museum of Anthropology and is probably the most recognisable object of Mesoamerican art.

events.title: The Templo Mayor at the centre of the Mexica world
events.summary: Rebuilt seven times, each shell enclosing the last, the great pyramid of Tenochtitlan carried twin shrines to Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain — the two things the state depended on. Its 1487 dedication was marked by mass human sacrifice, the numbers reported by both Mexica and Spanish sources being propaganda in opposite directions. Excavation under Mexico City since 1978 has recovered offerings from every province of the empire, buried in the platform.

events.title: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
events.summary: In early 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias, blown south by a storm, turned east and found open water beyond the southern tip of Africa, proving that the Indian Ocean could be reached by sea. Decades of Portuguese voyages down the West African coast, driven by the search for gold and a route to Asian spices, had led to this point. Vasco da Gama followed the route to India in 1498, and Portugal built a maritime empire on it.

events.title: 1492: Granada falls, Iberia transformed
events.summary: In January 1492 the emirate of Granada surrenders to Ferdinand and Isabella, ending nearly eight centuries of Muslim polities in Iberia. The same year the monarchs expel Spain's Jews, and Columbus sails west under their flag; within decades the Moriscos face forced conversion too. Militant religious unity and Atlantic expansion together forge the first empire on which, its kings boasted, the sun never set.

events.title: Columbus reaches the Americas
events.summary: On 12 October 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Castile, landed in the Bahamas, opening sustained contact between Europe and the Americas. The continents had been inhabited for at least fifteen thousand years and Norse sailors had reached Newfoundland around 1000, so this was not a discovery for the people already there. Its consequences were global: the exchange of crops, animals and diseases, the collapse of Indigenous populations, and the Atlantic slave trade and colonial empires that followed.

events.title: Askia Muhammad reorganises the Songhai Empire
events.summary: Seizing power after Sunni Ali's death, Askia Muhammad turned a conquest state into an administered one: provinces under appointed governors, a standing army and river fleet separated from the farming population, standard weights and measures, and Islamic law applied through trained judges. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1497 brought back the title of caliph of the Sudan. He made Timbuktu's scholars partners in government, and Songhai reached its greatest extent under him before his sons deposed him in 1528.

events.title: Timbuktu's manuscript culture under Songhai
events.summary: Under Askia Muhammad's Songhai empire, Timbuktu's Sankore mosque and private libraries make the city a university town of the Islamic world: jurists, astronomers and grammarians produce and copy manuscripts by the tens of thousands, traded by weight of gold. Hundreds of thousands of these texts survive in family collections today — standing refutation of the myth that sub-Saharan Africa lacked written scholarship.

events.title: The Treaty of Tordesillas divides the unknown world
events.summary: Two years after Columbus returned, Portugal and Castile agreed to split everything outside Christian Europe along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands — Portuguese to the east, Castilian to the west — with the pope's blessing and no consultation of anyone who lived there. The line gave Portugal its route to India and, as it turned out, Brazil, which is why Brazilians speak Portuguese. No means existed to measure longitude, so where the line actually fell was argued over for centuries.

events.title: Vasco da Gama opens the sea route to India
events.summary: Four ships left Lisbon, swung far out into the South Atlantic to catch the westerlies, rounded the Cape, worked up the Swahili coast and took on a pilot at Malindi who brought them across the Indian Ocean to Calicut in May 1498. The cargo they brought back paid for the voyage many times over. Within fifteen years Portugal had fortified posts from Mozambique to Malacca, and the spice trade that had run through Venice and Cairo for centuries began to shift to the Atlantic.

events.title: Portugal reaches Brazil and rounds the world's sea lanes
events.summary: Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival in Calicut opens the sea route to India that Portugal has sought for eighty years of African coasting; two years later Cabral, swinging wide on the same route, strikes Brazil. A small kingdom of a million people briefly runs a trading empire from Lisbon to Malacca and Macau, and the Portuguese language is planted on four continents, where it remains.

events.title: Guru Nanak's teaching and the founding of the Khalsa
events.summary: Guru Nanak, born in Punjab in 1469, began teaching around 1499 that there is one God, that all people are equal regardless of caste or creed, and that honest work, sharing and remembrance of God are the path to liberation. Nine Gurus followed; the fifth compiled the scripture and built the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar, and in 1699 the tenth, Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa order, after which the scripture itself became the eternal Guru. Sikhs number about 25 million today.

events.title: The Mexica send every child to school
events.summary: Mexica society expected all children, girls included and commoners as well as nobles, to attend a school. The telpochcalli of each district trained the young in work, warfare, civic duty and song; the calmecac attached to the temples taught the sons of nobles and promising commoners writing, the calendar, rhetoric, law and ritual, under harsh discipline. Few if any societies anywhere before the modern era attempted universal schooling. The description comes largely from post-conquest sources compiled from Nahua informants.

events.title: The Safavids make Iran Shia
events.summary: In 1501 Ismail I, head of a Sufi order, took Tabriz and proclaimed himself shah, making Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, until then mostly Sunni, and importing Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it. Under Abbas I after 1588 the capital Isfahan became one of the world's most beautiful cities. The Safavid conversion created the Sunni-Shia divide between Iran and its Ottoman and Uzbek neighbours that still shapes Middle Eastern politics.

events.title: Albuquerque takes Malacca and the eastern spice route
events.summary: Afonso de Albuquerque's small fleet stormed the sultanate that controlled the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the busiest entrepôt in Asia. With Goa taken the year before and Hormuz soon after, Portugal held the three chokepoints of the eastern trade and could tax or stop anyone passing. From Malacca Portuguese ships reached the Moluccas, China and, in 1543, Japan. The sultanate's successors at Johor fought back for a century.

events.title: The first printed Armenian book
events.summary: Hakob Meghapart printed Urbatagirk, the Book of Friday, in Venice — the earliest book set in Armenian type, sixty years after Gutenberg and while Armenia itself lay between the Ottoman and Safavid empires. Printing for a stateless people was done in diaspora: Armenian presses followed in Constantinople, Rome, Lviv, Amsterdam, Isfahan and Madras, where the first Armenian periodical appeared in 1794. The press kept the written language and its literature alive through three centuries without a state.

events.title: The Piri Reis map
events.summary: An Ottoman admiral compiled a world map on gazelle parchment from twenty older charts, including, he wrote in a marginal note, one drawn by Columbus. The surviving third shows the Atlantic with Iberia, West Africa and the coast of Brazil, annotated with what he knew of the voyages. It is one of the earliest maps of the Americas to survive and the only trace of the lost Columbus chart. Piri Reis also wrote the Kitab-i Bahriye, a detailed sailing guide to the Mediterranean.

events.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses and the Reformation
events.summary: In October 1517 the Augustinian friar Martin Luther circulated ninety-five theses attacking the sale of indulgences, an act tradition places on the door of the castle church at Wittenberg. His insistence on scripture and faith alone, spread by the new printing presses, split western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, was taken up by Zwingli, Calvin and the English crown, and set off more than a century of religious wars. The Catholic Church answered with its own Counter-Reformation.

events.title: The first circumnavigation of the Earth
events.summary: Five ships left Spain under Ferdinand Magellan in 1519 seeking a western route to the Spice Islands; they found the strait at the tip of South America, crossed the Pacific, and Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522 with eighteen survivors of about 270 men, completing the first voyage around the world. It demonstrated the true size of the Pacific and the globe and revealed the problem of the international date line.

events.title: The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent
events.summary: Suleiman I, sultan from 1520 to 1566, took Belgrade, Rhodes and most of Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529, and extended Ottoman power over Iraq, the Red Sea and North Africa. Known in Turkish as the Lawgiver, he reorganised the empire's legal code; his architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque. The Ottoman state, a multi-religious empire ruling millions of Christians and Jews under the millet system, remained one of the world's great powers into the eighteenth century.

events.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
events.summary: Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital on an island in Lake Texcoco and one of the largest cities in the world, fell to Hernán Cortés on 13 August 1521 after a siege of three months. The Spaniards' several hundred soldiers were joined by tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, and by a smallpox epidemic that had killed the emperor Cuitláhuac. Mexico City rose on the ruins, and the conquest opened three centuries of Spanish rule in the Americas.

events.title: The Atlantic slave trade at industrial scale
events.summary: From the first direct Africa-to-Americas voyage in 1526 to the last recorded landing in 1867, European traders — Portuguese and Brazilian ships above all — forcibly transport about 12.5 million Africans; nearly two million die at sea. Plantation slavery builds the Atlantic economy's sugar, tobacco and cotton wealth, devastates African societies, and creates the African diaspora whose descendants shape the culture of the Americas.

events.title: The transatlantic slave trade
events.summary: The first slave ship sailed directly from Africa to the Americas in 1526; the last documented voyage landed in Cuba in 1867. In between, European and American traders carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, of whom nearly two million died at sea, to work plantations of sugar, tobacco and cotton in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. It was the largest forced migration in history, devastated West and Central African societies, and shaped the demography and racial politics of the Americas.

events.title: A dynastic war leaves the Inca empire divided
events.summary: The emperor Huayna Capac and his designated heir died within days of each other, probably of smallpox spreading south ahead of the Spanish themselves. His sons Huascar in Cusco and Atahualpa in Quito fought a five-year war that ended with Atahualpa's generals capturing Cusco and executing his brother's family. Pizarro landed months later, into a state exhausted, purged of experienced commanders and full of provinces with a grievance — which is much of the explanation for what followed.

events.title: The Ethiopian-Adal war nearly ends the Christian kingdom
events.summary: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, remembered as Gran, led the sultanate of Adal out of the eastern lowlands with Ottoman firearms and overran most of the Ethiopian highlands, burning churches and monastic libraries as he went. Emperor Lebna Dengel died a fugitive. A small Portuguese musketeer force sent from Goa turned the balance; Ahmad was killed in battle in 1543 and Adal collapsed. Both states were left exhausted, and the Oromo migrations reshaped the region in the vacuum.

events.title: Pizarro seizes Atahualpa; the Inca state falls
events.summary: Arriving amid a devastating smallpox epidemic and a war of succession, Francisco Pizarro ambushes the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532, extorts a room full of gold, and executes him anyway. Cusco falls the next year, though a rump Inca state resists at Vilcabamba until 1572. Andean silver then powers the Spanish empire, while Quechua, the Inca lingua franca, remains spoken by millions.

events.title: The Neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba is extinguished
events.summary: Manco Inca, installed by the Spanish as a puppet, rebelled, besieged Cusco and then withdrew into the forested mountains northwest of it, where he and his sons kept an independent Inca state for thirty-six years, raiding the highways and negotiating with viceroys. Viceroy Toledo ended it: Vilcabamba was taken and the last ruler, Tupac Amaru, beheaded in Cusco's main square in 1572 before a crowd that reportedly wept. Andean resistance continued, but the Inca line of rulers stopped there.

events.title: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
events.summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, printed in Nuremberg in 1543, the year of his death, argued that the Earth turns daily on its axis and orbits the Sun with the other planets. The model was mathematically no simpler than Ptolemy's at first, but it explained retrograde motion naturally and opened the way for Kepler's elliptical orbits and Galileo's telescopic evidence. The Church placed the book on the Index in 1616.

events.title: Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica
events.summary: Andreas Vesalius, a Flemish physician teaching at Padua, published in 1543 an illustrated anatomy based on his own dissections of human bodies rather than on the ancient authority of Galen, whose descriptions had often come from animals. The Fabrica's precise woodcuts corrected hundreds of errors and set a new standard: knowledge of the body was to come from looking at the body. It appeared the same year as Copernicus's book, a coincidence often taken to mark the start of modern science.

events.title: Epidemic disease empties central Mexico
events.summary: Smallpox had arrived with the conquest; what the Nahua called cocoliztli, pestilence, came afterwards in waves, the worst in 1545 and 1576, with fever and bleeding that Spanish physicians did not recognise. Estimates suggest central Mexico's population fell by something like eighty to ninety per cent across the century. DNA recovered from a 1545 cemetery in Oaxaca has identified a strain of Salmonella enterica, probably introduced, as one agent; the question is not closed.

events.title: Spanish silver links the world's economies
events.summary: The silver mountain of Potosí, discovered in 1545, and the Manila galleons sailing yearly from 1571 connect American mines to Chinese markets: Spanish pesos become the first global money, so trusted that China's economy runs on them. The trade knits four continents into one economic system for the first time — at brutal human cost in the mines — and the peso's descendants include the U.S. dollar sign.

events.title: Ivan IV is crowned tsar of all Russia
events.summary: At sixteen Ivan took the title tsar — the Slavic form of caesar — claiming for Moscow the inheritance of the fallen Byzantine empire. His early reign brought a law code, a national assembly, a printing press and the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan, which opened the Volga to the Caspian. The later years brought the oprichnina terror, the sack of Novgorod, a ruinous Baltic war and the killing of his own heir, leaving the country to the anarchy of the Time of Troubles.

events.title: Mimar Sinan perfects the Ottoman dome
events.summary: Recruited as a boy through the devshirme levy and trained as a military engineer, Sinan became chief court architect for fifty years and is credited with several hundred buildings. The Suleymaniye in Istanbul and, at eighty-odd, the Selimiye at Edirne solved the problem he had worked at all his life: a single dome over an undivided space, carried on eight piers, that at Edirne finally exceeded Hagia Sophia's span. He also built aqueducts, bridges and baths, and trained the architects of the Taj Mahal's tradition.

events.title: The Valladolid debate argues whether conquest can be just
events.summary: Charles V suspended new conquests in the Americas and had the question argued before a royal junta. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda held that the indigenous peoples were natural slaves whom Spain could rightly subdue; Bartolomé de las Casas, a former encomendero turned bishop, argued they were rational human beings with rights, sovereigns of their own lands, and that the conquest was unjust. No verdict was issued. It is nonetheless the first formal European debate on the rights of colonised peoples, and it fed the beginnings of international law.

events.title: The Peace of Augsburg lets rulers choose the religion
events.summary: After three decades of confessional war inside the empire, Charles V's brother Ferdinand agreed with the imperial estates that each prince could establish either Catholicism or Lutheranism in his own territory, with subjects who disagreed free to emigrate. Calvinists were not covered, which stored up the conflict that became the Thirty Years' War. It was not toleration in the modern sense, but it was the first durable legal recognition in Europe that one realm need not have one faith.

events.title: The Florentine Codex records the Nahua world
events.summary: The Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagun spent decades in Tlatelolco interviewing Nahua elders through trilingual students who wrote their answers in Nahuatl, then set a Spanish version alongside it in parallel columns with over two thousand illustrations. Twelve books cover the gods, astronomy, rhetoric, commerce, plants, animals, medicine and the conquest told from the Mexica side. Philip II ordered such work suppressed and the manuscript went to Florence. It is the fullest record of any pre-Columbian culture, largely in its own words.

events.title: Akbar's policy of religious tolerance in Mughal India
events.summary: The Mughal emperor Akbar, ruling from 1556 to 1605, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564, took Hindu Rajput princesses as wives, appointed Hindus to high office and from 1575 convened debates among Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit scholars at Fatehpur Sikri. His policy of sulh-i-kul, peace with all, made the Mughal state an empire of diverse subjects rather than a Muslim conquest state; it was reversed by his great-grandson Aurangzeb.

events.title: Russia crosses Siberia to the Pacific
events.summary: A Cossack band under Yermak, financed by the Stroganov merchant house, crossed the Urals after sable fur and broke the khanate of Sibir. Travelling by river and portage and building stockaded forts as they went, small parties covered the width of Asia in under sixty years and reached the Pacific at Okhotsk in 1639. Fur tribute paid for it, indigenous peoples were taxed and decimated by disease, and Russia acquired the territorial shape it still has.

events.title: The Spanish Armada is defeated
events.summary: Philip II sends some 130 ships to escort an invasion army from Flanders and bring England back to Catholic obedience. Harried up the Channel by faster English guns, scattered by fireships at Calais and battered at Gravelines, the Armada flees north around Scotland into Atlantic gales that wreck dozens of ships on Irish shores; barely half the fleet limps home. Spain remains the superpower for decades yet, but England's survival announces the sea power that will shape the coming centuries.

events.title: Gunpowder ends the Songhai Empire at Tondibi
events.summary: The Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent an army of a few thousand across the Sahara, many of them Iberian renegades and captives armed with arquebuses and small cannon, to seize the Niger gold trade. At Tondibi north of Gao they broke a far larger Songhai force whose cavalry and infantry had no answer to massed firearms. The largest state in West African history fragmented within a few years, the scholars of Timbuktu were deported, and the Saharan trade routes never recovered their old importance.

events.title: Korea repels the Japanese Imjin invasions
events.summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi hurls Japan's battle-hardened armies at Korea in 1592, aiming through it at Ming China. Seoul and Pyongyang fall within months, but admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet — with its armoured turtle ships — strangles the invasion's supply lines, winning at Hansan Island and, with thirteen ships against well over a hundred, at Myeongnyang. Ming intervention and guerrilla 'righteous armies' grind the war to stalemate; Hideyoshi's death ends it. Korea is devastated but unconquered, and Yi becomes its greatest hero.

events.title: The Edict of Nantes grants the Huguenots toleration
events.summary: Henry IV, a Protestant who had converted to win Paris, ended thirty-six years of religious war by granting French Calvinists freedom of conscience, public worship in specified places, full civil rights and about a hundred fortified towns of their own. It was a settlement between armed parties rather than a principle, and it worked: France recovered. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, driving perhaps two hundred thousand skilled Huguenots into England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia and the American colonies.

events.title: Shakespeare writes for the Globe
events.summary: A glover's son from Stratford became actor, shareholder and resident playwright of a London company that opened the Globe on Bankside in 1599. Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth were written for that stage and that repertory of players, for audiences paying a penny to stand. Thirty-six plays were collected by his colleagues in the First Folio of 1623, without which half of them would be lost. He is credited with introducing or fixing hundreds of English words and phrases still in daily use.

events.title: Sekigahara and the Tokugawa peace
events.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara in 1600 ends a century of civil war; three years later he is shogun, ruling from Edo — the future Tokyo. The Tokugawa order fixes society into ranks, expels missionaries and closes the country to most foreign contact, and then presides over two and a half centuries of peace in which cities, literacy, kabuki and ukiyo-e printmaking flourish.

events.title: The Tokugawa shogunate closes Japan
events.summary: After Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war, his successors banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese and by 1639 confined foreign trade to a Dutch post at Nagasaki and to Chinese, Korean and Ryukyuan channels. The policy later called sakoku kept Japan largely isolated from the West for over two centuries of internal peace, urban growth and flourishing arts, until American warships forced the ports open in 1853.

events.title: Cervantes publishes Don Quixote
events.summary: A maimed veteran of Lepanto, five years a captive in Algiers and twice jailed as a tax collector, wrote a parody of chivalric romance about an elderly reader who believes what he reads. The joke turned into something else: characters who change, who have read the first volume of their own story, and a narrator who is not to be trusted. It is commonly called the first modern novel, was translated within a decade, and has never gone out of print in four hundred years.

events.title: Galileo turns the telescope on the sky
events.summary: Having improved the newly invented Dutch telescope, Galileo Galilei published Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610, reporting mountains on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way and four moons circling Jupiter, proof that not everything orbits the Earth. His later observations of the phases of Venus supported Copernicus. Tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for defending the Sun-centred system, he spent his last years under house arrest, where he wrote his foundational work on motion and mechanics.

events.title: The Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia
events.summary: Beginning with a Protestant revolt in Bohemia in 1618, the war drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain and devastated Germany, where perhaps a fifth of the population died of violence, famine and disease. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 settled the religious map of the Holy Roman Empire and recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic and Swiss Confederation. It is often, if loosely, taken as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states.

events.title: Bacon, Descartes and the Royal Society
events.summary: Francis Bacon's Novum Organum of 1620 argued that knowledge of nature should be built up by systematic observation and experiment, and René Descartes's Discourse on the Method of 1637 by reasoning from clear first principles. The Royal Society of London, founded in 1660 with the motto 'take nobody's word for it', and the Académie des Sciences in Paris in 1666 institutionalised experiment, publication and peer scrutiny. Together they defined the methods that Newton's generation would use.

events.title: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal
events.summary: The Mughal emperor buried his wife Mumtaz Mahal, dead in childbirth, under a white marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra, set at the end rather than the centre of a four-part garden so that it is reflected in the whole length of the water channel. Craftsmen inlaid semiprecious stone into the marble in flowering patterns and worked Quranic calligraphy that is graded in size to read evenly from the ground. Twenty thousand workers and two decades went into it.

events.title: Fasilides founds Gondar and builds its castles
events.summary: After centuries in which Ethiopian emperors had ruled from moving tent camps, Fasilides settled his court north of Lake Tana and enclosed it in a stone compound of castles, banqueting halls, libraries and baths, built in a style that fuses Ethiopian, Nubian and Indian and Portuguese elements. Gondar became a city of forty thousand and a centre of painting and manuscript production for two hundred years, until the era of regional warlords known as the Zemene Mesafint dispersed its authority.

events.title: The English Civil War and the execution of a king
events.summary: A quarrel over taxation, religion and whether parliament could be dispensed with became nine years of war across England, Scotland and Ireland. Cromwell's New Model Army beat the royalists, and in January 1649 Charles I was tried by a court his own subjects constituted and beheaded in Whitehall — a king killed by law rather than by murder. The republic that followed lasted eleven years before the monarchy returned, but no English ruler afterwards tried to govern without parliament for long.

events.title: Leeuwenhoek observes microorganisms
events.summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft cloth merchant who ground tiny, powerful single lenses, reported to the Royal Society in 1676 that a drop of pepper water swarmed with 'little animals', the first observation of bacteria and protozoa. Robert Hooke's Micrographia of 1665 had already coined the word cell. Leeuwenhoek went on to describe red blood cells, sperm and muscle fibres. Their work revealed a living world invisible to the naked eye, though its link to disease waited two centuries.

events.title: Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles
events.summary: The king turned his father's hunting lodge into a palace for ten thousand people, with Le Vau and Hardouin-Mansart building and Le Nôtre laying out gardens whose fountains needed a river diverted and a vast pumping machine to feed them. Moving the government there took the nobility out of their provinces and put them in daily competition for the king's attention — politics reduced to etiquette. Every court in Europe copied the architecture, and French became the language of diplomacy.

events.title: The Ottoman tide turns at Vienna
events.summary: Kara Mustafa's army had mined its way close to the walls after two months when a relief force of Habsburg, German and Polish troops came over the Kahlenberg hills, ending the day with a massed charge of Polish winged hussars under Jan III Sobieski. The siege collapsed and the grand vizier was executed. The Holy League's counter-offensive took Hungary within sixteen years, and the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 was the first in which the Ottomans conceded substantial territory.

events.title: Newton publishes the Principia
events.summary: Isaac Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in London in 1687, set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, showing that the same force that pulls an apple to the ground holds the Moon and planets in their orbits. It unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics with mathematics and remained the framework of physics until Einstein. The book drew on Kepler, Galileo and Hooke, and on the calculus Newton and Leibniz developed independently.

events.title: England's Glorious Revolution and Bill of Rights
events.summary: Parliament's invitation brings William of Orange to England; James II flees, and the crown passes on conditions. The 1689 Bill of Rights bars taxation or standing armies without Parliament, guarantees free elections and parliamentary speech, and settles that monarchs rule under law. Joined to the Bank of England and a free-ish press, the settlement creates the constitutional and financial machinery of Britain's rise.

events.title: The English Bill of Rights
events.summary: After the Glorious Revolution deposed James II, Parliament made William and Mary's accession conditional on a Declaration of Rights, enacted in December 1689. It forbade the monarch to suspend laws, levy taxes or keep a standing army without Parliament, guaranteed free elections and free speech in Parliament, and banned cruel and unusual punishments and excessive bail. It established parliamentary supremacy in Britain and was a direct model for the American Bill of Rights a century later.

events.title: Peter the Great turns Russia toward Europe
events.summary: Travelling west incognito to study shipbuilding, Peter returns to drag Russia into Europe: a navy from nothing, a conscript army that finally beats Sweden at Poltava, state service open to merit, a simplified alphabet, and a new capital — St Petersburg — built on conquered Baltic marshland. He proclaims Russia an empire in 1721; its ambivalence between European identity and its own path dates from his reign.

events.title: The last independent Maya kingdom falls
events.summary: The Itza kingdom on an island in Lake Peten Itza, in what is now northern Guatemala, held out for a hundred and seventy years after the fall of the Aztec capital, protected by forest and swamp and by its own prophetic calendar, which set the date at which submission would be acceptable. A Spanish force built a galley, crossed the lake and took Nojpeten in March 1697. It is the latest date at which any indigenous American state lost its independence to the conquest.

events.title: The British Agricultural Revolution
events.summary: Over the eighteenth century English and Dutch farmers raised yields with crop rotations that replaced fallow with turnips and clover, selective breeding of livestock, enclosure of open fields, and tools such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of about 1701. Output per worker rose enough to feed growing cities and free labour for factories, a precondition of the Industrial Revolution. Enclosure also dispossessed many rural poor, and the balance between its gains and costs remains argued.

events.title: The steam engine, from Newcomen to Watt
events.summary: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine of 1712 pumped water from English coal mines, the first practical machine to turn heat into work. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769 and first installed commercially in 1776, cut its fuel use by three-quarters, and his rotary engines of the 1780s could drive mills and factories anywhere. Steam power freed industry from rivers and muscle, and its later applications to locomotives and ships transformed transport within a lifetime.

events.title: Ibrahim Muteferrika opens the first Ottoman Turkish press
events.summary: A Hungarian convert in Ottoman service obtained a decree from Ahmed III and a fatwa permitting printing in Turkish on secular subjects — religious texts remained the copyists' preserve. His press in Istanbul issued seventeen works in Arabic script between 1729 and 1742: dictionaries, histories, geography with printed maps, and his own treatise urging the empire to study European military methods. Armenian, Greek and Jewish presses had worked in the city since the 1490s; this was the first for the language of the state.

events.title: Linnaeus names the living world
events.summary: The Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in 1735 and, in its tenth edition of 1758, gave every animal a two-word Latin name of genus and species, the binomial system still used for all organisms, and sorted them into a nested hierarchy of classes and orders. He placed humans among the primates as Homo sapiens. His classification was artificial in places and his ideas on human races have been repudiated, but his naming system made global biology possible.

events.title: The Encyclopédie and the Enlightenment
events.summary: Edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert and published in 28 volumes between 1751 and 1772 despite censorship, the Encyclopédie set out to gather all human knowledge, from crafts and machines to philosophy, and to subject religion, government and tradition to reason. Its 70,000 articles by Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and others carried the Enlightenment's confidence in progress, tolerance and natural rights to readers across Europe and the Americas, preparing the ground for the revolutions that followed.

events.title: The Lisbon earthquake and the birth of seismology
events.summary: On All Saints' morning a great offshore earthquake, a tsunami and three days of fire destroyed one of Europe's richest capitals and killed tens of thousands in their churches. The marquis of Pombal rebuilt the centre to a grid with the first purpose-designed anti-seismic timber cages, and circulated a questionnaire to every parish about the shaking, its direction and duration — the first systematic earthquake survey. The disaster also forced a European argument about providence that runs through Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant.

events.title: Mechanised cotton spinning and the factory
events.summary: James Hargreaves's spinning jenny of about 1764, Richard Arkwright's water frame patented in 1769 and installed in his Cromford mill in 1771, Samuel Crompton's mule of 1779 and Edmund Cartwright's power loom of 1785 mechanised textile production in Lancashire and Derbyshire. Cotton spun by machines in factories, fed by slave-grown American cotton and powered first by water and then steam, was the leading sector of the Industrial Revolution, which within a century remade work, cities and the world economy.

events.title: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations
events.summary: Published in March 1776, Adam Smith's Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations explained how the division of labour raises productivity, how prices coordinate self-interested actors as if by an invisible hand, and why mercantilist restrictions on trade impoverish nations. It founded economics as a discipline and supplied the case for free markets and free trade, while also warning against monopolies and the deadening effect of repetitive work.

events.title: The United States Declaration of Independence
events.summary: Adopted by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776 and drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, the Declaration announced the separation of thirteen British colonies and asserted that all men are created equal, endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Its author and many signers held slaves, a contradiction its later readers, from abolitionists to Lincoln, turned against slavery itself.

events.title: Tupac Amaru II rises against colonial Peru
events.summary: A wealthy indigenous curaca who claimed descent from the last Inca took his ancestor's name, executed a hated provincial governor and raised tens of thousands across the southern Andes against the mit'a drafts, forced sales and new taxes. It was the largest revolt in colonial Spanish America. He was captured, forced to watch his family die and torn apart in the square where Tupac Amaru had been beheaded. The Crown banned Inca dress, titles and the Quechua theatre; his name became a byword for resistance.

events.title: The US Constitution and Bill of Rights
events.summary: Drafted at Philadelphia in 1787 and in force from 1789, the Constitution created a federal republic with separated legislative, executive and judicial powers and is the oldest written national constitution still in use. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, guarantee freedom of religion, speech, press and assembly, jury trial and due process. It counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation; the Thirteenth to Fifteenth Amendments after the Civil War began to repair that.

events.title: Lavoisier founds modern chemistry
events.summary: By weighing everything, including the gases, Lavoisier showed that burning is combination with oxygen rather than the release of a substance called phlogiston, that water is hydrogen and oxygen combined, and that matter is conserved through chemical change. His 1789 textbook listed the known elements and introduced the systematic naming chemistry still uses, much of it worked out with his collaborator and wife Marie-Anne Paulze. The Revolution he had supported guillotined him in 1794 for his work as a tax farmer.

events.title: The French Revolution and the Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.summary: Weeks after the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789, the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, proclaiming that men are born free and equal in rights, that sovereignty lies in the nation, and that law is the expression of the general will. The Revolution abolished feudal privilege, executed the king, passed through the Terror and ended with Napoleon's coup in 1799; its declaration shaped constitutions and rights movements worldwide.

events.title: The Haitian Revolution
events.summary: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in August 1791 and, under leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeated French, Spanish and British forces over thirteen years. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804, the only state founded by a successful slave revolt and the second independent nation in the Americas. The revolution ended slavery there, alarmed slaveholding powers across the Atlantic world, and inspired abolitionists for decades.

events.title: Vaccination against smallpox
events.summary: Inoculation with material from smallpox pustules to induce a mild case had long been practised in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and West Africa, and was brought to Britain by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in 1721 and to Boston by an enslaved man, Onesimus. In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that the milder cowpox protected against smallpox, a safer method he named vaccination. Vaccination programmes eradicated smallpox worldwide in 1980, the only human disease so far eliminated.

events.title: The Louisiana Purchase doubles the United States
events.summary: Napoleon, having lost his army in Haiti and needing money for a European war, offered the whole of French Louisiana rather than just New Orleans; Jefferson's envoys took it for about fifteen million dollars, roughly four cents an acre for two million square kilometres. Jefferson doubted the constitution allowed it and did it anyway. Thirteen future states came out of the territory, along with a century of dispossession of the nations already living there and a bitter argument over whether slavery would follow.

events.title: The Napoleonic Wars
events.summary: From 1803 to his final defeat at Waterloo in 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte's France fought successive coalitions across Europe, from Lisbon to Moscow, in wars that killed several million people. He redrew the map of the continent, spread the metric system and his civil code, and ended the Holy Roman Empire. His sale of Louisiana doubled the United States, and his occupation of Spain triggered the independence wars of Spanish America. The Congress of Vienna's settlement kept a general European peace for forty years.

events.title: The Napoleonic Code
events.summary: Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 states private law in plain numbered articles: equality before the law, freedom of contract, secure property, civil marriage — while rolling back revolutionary gains for women. Carried by French armies and imitated voluntarily afterwards, it becomes the most influential law book since Justinian, shaping the civil codes of continental Europe, Latin America, Quebec, Louisiana, Egypt and Japan.

events.title: The Holy Roman Empire is dissolved
events.summary: After Austerlitz, Napoleon organised sixteen German states into a Confederation of the Rhine under his protection, and on 6 August 1806 Francis II laid down the imperial crown rather than see it taken, releasing every remaining member from its obligations. A polity founded in 962 simply stopped existing. The hundreds of small principalities and free cities had already been swept together in the mediatisation of 1803, and the ground was cleared for the Austro-Prussian rivalry that produced modern Germany.

events.title: Britain abolishes the Atlantic slave trade
events.summary: After two decades of campaigning by abolitionists — Wilberforce in Parliament, Clarkson on the road, Equiano in print, and hundreds of thousands of petitioners — Britain outlaws its slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself across most of the empire in 1833. The Royal Navy's squadrons then police the Atlantic. Abolition is incomplete and self-interested readings persist, but a major power has turned against the traffic it once dominated.

events.title: Independence of Spanish America
events.summary: With Spain occupied by Napoleon, juntas across the Americas claimed self-rule from 1810. Fifteen years of war followed, led in the north by Simón Bolívar and in the south by José de San Martín, whose armies met in Peru; Mexico won independence in 1821 and the last royalist forces surrendered in 1826. Brazil separated peacefully from Portugal in 1822. Nearly all of the mainland Americas was independent by 1825, though slavery persisted in Brazil and Cuba for decades.

events.title: The Cádiz Constitution
events.summary: With Napoleon's armies holding most of Spain, a parliament meeting in besieged Cádiz wrote a constitution vesting sovereignty in the nation, creating a single chamber elected by near-universal male suffrage including the American territories, guaranteeing press freedom and abolishing seigneurial jurisdiction and the Inquisition. Nicknamed La Pepa, it was repealed by Ferdinand VII in 1814 and twice revived. It was a model for liberal constitutions from Portugal and Naples to the new republics of Spanish America.

events.title: Champollion deciphers Egyptian hieroglyphs
events.summary: Working from the trilingual Rosetta Stone, Jean-François Champollion announces in 1822 that hieroglyphs record a real language — ancient Egyptian — mixing phonetic and ideographic signs. Three thousand years of inscriptions, from pyramid texts to temple walls, abruptly become readable, founding Egyptology and restoring to Egypt a written history longer than any other then known. The stone itself had been found by French soldiers in 1799.

events.title: The Trail of Tears
events.summary: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 gave the president authority to trade eastern homelands for territory west of the Mississippi, and the Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw were marched out, most under military escort. The Supreme Court ruled in the Cherokee's favour in Worcester v. Georgia and the ruling was ignored. Thousands died of cold, hunger and disease on the way; the Cherokee alone lost perhaps a quarter of those removed. Around 60,000 people were displaced.

events.title: The first inter-city passenger railway
events.summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830, the first line to carry passengers and goods on a timetable between two cities entirely by steam locomotive, after George and Robert Stephenson's Rocket had won the Rainhill Trials the year before. A member of Parliament was killed by a train on opening day. Railways spread across Britain, Europe, India and the Americas within decades, collapsing distance, creating national markets and standard time.

events.title: Hokusai prints the Great Wave
events.summary: The opening sheet of Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji is a colour woodblock print of a breaking wave with clawed foam, three cargo boats beneath it and Fuji small on the horizon. Thousands of impressions were pulled and sold for the price of a bowl of noodles. When Japanese prints reached Europe after 1853 they changed the way Monet, Degas, van Gogh and Debussy composed. It is probably the most reproduced image ever made in Asia.

events.title: Britain abolishes slavery in its empire
events.summary: Twenty-six years after outlawing the slave trade, Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in August 1833, freeing about 800,000 enslaved people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape from 1834, though most were bound to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' first, and slaveholders, not the enslaved, were paid compensation. It followed decades of campaigning by Black abolitionists such as Olaudah Equiano, mass petitions, and the 1831 uprising in Jamaica. France abolished slavery in 1848, the United States in 1865, Brazil in 1888.

events.title: The electric telegraph
events.summary: Cooke and Wheatstone in England and Samuel Morse in the United States patented working electric telegraphs in 1837; Morse's line from Washington to Baltimore opened in 1844 with the message 'What hath God wrought'. For the first time information travelled faster than a horse or a ship. The first lasting transatlantic cable was completed in 1866, and by the 1870s cables linked Europe to India, Australia and the Americas, wiring together markets, empires and newspapers.

events.title: The First Opium War
events.summary: When the Qing official Lin Zexu destroyed British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain sent a fleet whose steam gunboats and modern artillery overwhelmed Chinese defences. The Treaty of Nanking in 1842 ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports to foreign trade and residence and imposed an indemnity, the first of the 'unequal treaties'. The war began a century in which China lost sovereignty piece by piece to Western powers and Japan, a period Chinese historiography calls the century of humiliation.

events.title: The Tanzimat: Ottoman reform and equal citizenship
events.summary: Beginning with the Gülhane edict of 1839, Ottoman statesmen legislate security of life and property, tax and conscription reform, secular schools and courts, and — radically — legal equality of Muslim and non-Muslim subjects, capped by the 1876 constitution and parliament. The reforms strain against debt, nationalism and autocratic reaction, but they create the administrative and intellectual scaffolding of the modern Middle East's states.

events.title: The Treaty of Waitangi
events.summary: Over five hundred Maori chiefs signed an agreement with the British Crown that exists in two versions which do not say the same thing: the English text cedes sovereignty, the Maori text cedes kawanatanga, governorship, while guaranteeing tino rangatiratanga, full chiefly authority, over lands and treasures. A century and a half of land confiscation followed. The Waitangi Tribunal, established in 1975, now hears historical claims under it, and the treaty is treated as New Zealand's founding constitutional document.

events.title: Surgical anaesthesia
events.summary: On 16 October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital, William Morton administered ether while a surgeon removed a tumour from a patient's neck, the first public demonstration that surgery could be painless. Chloroform followed a year later in Edinburgh. Earlier claims exist, including Crawford Long's use of ether in 1842 and Hanaoka Seishū's herbal anaesthetic in Japan in 1804. Anaesthesia, with antisepsis two decades later, turned surgery from a desperate last resort into a routine treatment.

events.title: The Seneca Falls Convention and the Declaration of Sentiments
events.summary: The first women's rights convention, organised by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott in Seneca Falls, New York, in July 1848, adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modelled on the Declaration of Independence: all men and women are created equal. Its most contested resolution demanded the vote. It launched the organised women's suffrage movement in the United States; New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant women the vote in 1893, the United States in 1920.

events.title: The Taiping Rebellion
events.summary: Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus, led a millenarian movement that seized Nanjing in 1853 and ruled much of southern China as the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, abolishing foot-binding and private landholding in principle. Qing armies, regional militias and Western-officered forces retook Nanjing in 1864. With an estimated twenty to thirty million dead from war, famine and disease, it was the deadliest civil war in history.

events.title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.summary: Beginning with a mutiny of East India Company sepoys at Meerut in May 1857, the revolt spread across northern and central India, joined by princes, landowners and peasants with grievances against annexation, taxation and interference with religion. Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow saw massacres on both sides before British forces prevailed in 1858. The Company was abolished and India placed under the Crown; the rebellion is remembered in India as the first war of independence.

events.title: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
events.summary: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, published on 24 November 1859, argued that species change over time through natural selection acting on heritable variation, and that all living things share common ancestry. Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea independently, prompting a joint announcement the year before. Evolution by natural selection became the unifying theory of biology, and its implications for human origins provoked religious and social debate that continues.

events.title: Alexander II emancipates the serfs
events.summary: By the edict of 1861, some twenty-three million privately held serfs — nearly a third of Russia's population — gain personal freedom, two years before America's Emancipation Proclamation. The terms are grudging: peasants must redeem their allotments through decades of payments to communes, and rural poverty persists. Yet the greatest single act of emancipation in Europe's history opens Russia's road to modern courts, zemstvo councils and industry.

events.title: Germ theory of disease
events.summary: Louis Pasteur showed in 1861 that microorganisms cause fermentation and putrefaction and do not arise spontaneously; Joseph Lister applied the idea to surgery with carbolic antisepsis from 1867, and Robert Koch identified the bacteria of anthrax in 1876 and tuberculosis in 1882, setting out postulates for proving a microbe causes a disease. Ignaz Semmelweis had shown in 1847 that hand-washing prevented childbed fever, and was ignored. Germ theory underlies sanitation, vaccines and antibiotics.

events.title: The American Civil War and the end of slavery
events.summary: Eleven slaveholding states seceded after Abraham Lincoln's election, and war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861. Some 750,000 soldiers died, more than in all other American wars combined. The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in rebel states free, nearly 200,000 Black men served in Union forces, and the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the country in 1865, months after the Confederate surrender and Lincoln's assassination. Reconstruction's promise of equal citizenship was largely abandoned by 1877.

events.title: The Meiji Restoration
events.summary: In 1868 a coalition of samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and restored rule in the name of the young emperor Meiji. The new government abolished the feudal domains and samurai class, adopted a conscript army, universal schooling, railways, a Western-style constitution in 1889 and industrial policy, transforming Japan within a generation into the first non-Western industrial power, able to defeat China in 1895 and Russia in 1905.

events.title: Mendeleev's periodic table
events.summary: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by atomic weight so that similar properties recurred at intervals, and left gaps for elements not yet found, predicting the properties of gallium, scandium and germanium, all discovered within fifteen years. Lothar Meyer reached a similar table independently. The periodic law was later explained by atomic structure and reordered by atomic number; the table remains chemistry's organising chart, with 118 elements today.

events.title: The first transcontinental railroad is completed
events.summary: A golden spike at Promontory Summit in Utah joined track laid east from Sacramento to track laid west from Omaha, cutting a journey that had taken months by wagon to about a week. Most of the Central Pacific's workforce through the Sierra Nevada were Chinese labourers, who tunnelled and blasted in winter snowsheds for lower pay than white crews. The line opened the plains to settlement and cattle, hastened the destruction of the bison herds, and forced the country onto standard time zones.

events.title: Tolstoy publishes War and Peace
events.summary: Six years' work produced a book of some half a million words following five aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of 1812, with essays on history folded in between the scenes. Tolstoy argued that great men do not direct events but are carried by them, an attack on the whole idea of the decisive individual. Together with Dostoevsky's novels of the same decade it made nineteenth-century Russian fiction the standard against which the form has been measured since.

events.title: The Paris Commune
events.summary: After France's defeat by Prussia, Parisians refused to disarm, drove out the national government and for seventy-two days ran the city themselves: elected councillors on a worker's wage and recallable, free secular schooling, workshops handed to cooperatives, rents and debts suspended. The army retook Paris street by street in a bloody week that killed thousands and ended in mass executions and deportations. Marx and Lenin both treated it as the first workers' government, and it haunted European politics for generations.

events.title: The telephone and electric lighting
events.summary: Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone in March 1876, hours ahead of Elisha Gray's filing; Antonio Meucci and others had built earlier devices, and priority remains argued. Thomas Edison's long-lasting carbon-filament lamp of 1879, and Joseph Swan's parallel work in England, made electric light practical, and Edison's Pearl Street station in New York began supplying customers in 1882. Electricity grids, motors and the telephone reshaped cities and work within a generation.

events.title: Hebrew is revived as a spoken language
events.summary: Hebrew had been read, prayed and written for eighteen centuries without being anyone's mother tongue. From 1881 Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and a wider movement of teachers and settlers in Ottoman Palestine set out to change that, coining thousands of words for things the Bible never named and insisting on Hebrew-only schooling. By 1922 the British mandate recognised it as an official language. It is the only documented case of a language with no native speakers becoming the everyday tongue of millions.

events.title: The Berlin Conference and the scramble for Africa
events.summary: Fourteen European states and the United States met in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885 to set rules for claiming African territory; no African was present. Within twenty years almost the entire continent had been partitioned, often by force, with borders that cut across peoples and are largely those of today's states. The Congo Free State, King Leopold II's private domain recognised at Berlin, became notorious for atrocities that killed millions. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

events.title: The automobile
events.summary: Karl Benz's Patent-Motorwagen, a three-wheeled carriage driven by a single-cylinder petrol engine, was patented in January 1886 and is generally counted the first practical automobile; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a four-wheeled car the same year. Bertha Benz's 100-kilometre drive in 1888 was the first road trip. Henry Ford's moving assembly line of 1913 made cars affordable, and the automobile reshaped cities, landscapes, the oil industry and the atmosphere.

events.title: Brazil abolishes slavery
events.summary: On 13 May 1888 Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, freeing the roughly 700,000 people still enslaved in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery and the one that had received more enslaved Africans than any other, about four million. Abolition followed decades of flight, revolt and campaigning by Black and white abolitionists such as Luís Gama and Joaquim Nabuco. No compensation or land was provided to the freed; the monarchy fell the next year.

events.title: The Trans-Siberian Railway
events.summary: Nine thousand kilometres of track from Moscow to Vladivostok, laid across permafrost, taiga and the mountains around Lake Baikal, mostly by soldiers, convicts and contracted Chinese labourers. It is the longest railway line in the world. It carried several million settlers east, tied Siberia's grain and minerals to European Russia, moved the armies of two wars and a revolution, and turned a colonial hinterland into part of a single state. The Amur section was finished in 1916.

events.title: Ellis Island and the age of mass immigration
events.summary: For sixty-two years the federal inspection station in New York harbour processed arriving steerage passengers — twelve million people, at a peak of over a million a year, most cleared in a few hours after a medical check and a list of questions, about two per cent turned back. Something like a third of Americans have an ancestor who passed through it. The quota laws of 1921 and 1924 cut the flow sharply and by national origin, and the station closed in 1954.

events.title: New Zealand grants women the vote
events.summary: On 19 September 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all adult women, including Māori women, the right to vote in national elections, after petitions organised by Kate Sheppard gathered signatures from nearly a quarter of the adult female population. South Australia followed in 1894 and added the right to stand for parliament. Finland in 1906 was the first European country; most Western democracies enfranchised women after the First World War, Switzerland only in 1971.

events.title: The Donghak peasant revolution
events.summary: Farmers in the southwest, organised through the Donghak religious movement, rose against corrupt magistrates and foreign grain merchants, demanding an end to the slave registers, land redistribution and the burning of debt records. They beat government troops and briefly ran their own local councils. Seoul called in Chinese soldiers; Japan sent its own, and the First Sino-Japanese War was fought over Korea's head. The rising was crushed with tens of thousands killed, and Korea's independence did not survive the aftermath.

events.title: Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa
events.summary: On 1 March 1896 Emperor Menelik II's army — a coalition of Ethiopia's regions armed with modern rifles he had shrewdly stockpiled — destroys an invading Italian force at Adwa. Italy recognises Ethiopian independence; alone in Africa apart from Liberia, Ethiopia escapes the colonial partition. The victory reverberates for decades as proof African arms could defeat a European power, feeding later pan-African movements.

events.title: Radioactivity and the Curies
events.summary: Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium salts fogged photographic plates through paper; Marie and Pierre Curie showed the emission was a property of atoms, named it radioactivity, and in 1898 isolated two new elements, polonium and radium, from tonnes of pitchblende. Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry, the first person to win two. Radioactivity revealed that atoms could change, gave geologists a clock for the age of the Earth, and led to nuclear physics.

events.title: The first powered aeroplane flight
events.summary: On 17 December 1903 at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew the Wright Flyer for twelve seconds and 37 metres, the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air machine; the fourth flight that day lasted nearly a minute. The brothers' key insight was control in three axes, achieved by warping the wings. Within a decade aircraft crossed the Channel and served in war; within fifty years jet airliners crossed oceans in hours.

events.title: Einstein's annus mirabilis and special relativity
events.summary: In 1905, while working at the Swiss patent office, Albert Einstein published four papers: one explained the photoelectric effect with light quanta, one established the reality of atoms through Brownian motion, one introduced special relativity, in which space and time depend on the observer's motion and the speed of light is constant, and one derived the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc². General relativity, his theory of gravity as curved spacetime, followed in 1915.

events.title: Iran's Constitutional Revolution wins a parliament
events.summary: Merchants, clerics and reformers closed the bazaars and took sanctuary until the Qajar shah conceded an elected assembly, the Majlis, which met in 1906 and wrote a constitution limiting royal power and guaranteeing courts and a press. It was the first such movement in Asia's Middle East. A royalist coup shelled parliament in 1908, and Russian and British intervention smothered the revived assembly by 1911, but the Majlis and the idea of law above the crown became permanent features of Iranian politics.

events.title: The Haber–Bosch process
events.summary: Fritz Haber demonstrated in 1909 that nitrogen from the air could be combined with hydrogen into ammonia under high pressure over an iron catalyst, and Carl Bosch scaled it to an industrial plant at Oppau by 1913. Synthetic ammonia made cheap fertiliser possible; roughly half the nitrogen in the bodies of people alive today has passed through the process, which sustains several billion of them. It also supplied explosives for two world wars, and Haber directed Germany's chemical warfare.

events.title: The Mexican Revolution
events.summary: A revolt against the thirty-year dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz in 1910 became a decade of civil war among factions led by Francisco Madero, Emiliano Zapata, Pancho Villa and Venustiano Carranza, in which perhaps a million people died. The Constitution of 1917 that emerged was among the first to guarantee social rights: land reform, an eight-hour day, the right to strike and national ownership of subsoil resources. It influenced constitutions across Latin America and beyond.

events.title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole
events.summary: Roald Amundsen and four companions reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 using dog sleds and skis, techniques learned from Inuit and Sámi practice; Robert Falcon Scott's party arrived five weeks later and died on the return. The pole was the last of the great geographical goals on land. Its attainment closed the age of exploration that had begun with Polynesian and Portuguese navigators and left the deep sea and space as the remaining frontiers.

events.title: The Xinhai Revolution ends imperial China
events.summary: An uprising at Wuchang in October 1911 spread through the provinces, and in February 1912 the child emperor Puyi abdicated, ending the Qing dynasty and two thousand years of imperial rule. Sun Yat-sen briefly headed the new Republic of China before yielding to the general Yuan Shikai. The republic soon fragmented among warlords, but the revolution's ideas of nationalism and popular sovereignty shaped both the Nationalist and Communist movements that fought for China's future.

events.title: Plate tectonics is accepted
events.summary: Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had drifted apart from a single landmass, citing matching coastlines, fossils and rocks, but could offer no mechanism and was dismissed for decades. Mapping of the mid-ocean ridges, the discovery of sea-floor spreading by Harry Hess in 1962, and magnetic striping of the ocean floor led by 1968 to the theory of rigid plates moving over the mantle. Plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building and the shape of the Earth's surface.

events.title: The First World War
events.summary: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914 set off a chain of mobilisations that brought the European alliances to war by August. Machine guns, artillery and trenches produced stalemate on the Western Front and slaughter at Verdun and the Somme; fighting spread to the Middle East, Africa and the seas, and colonial troops served in millions. Around nine million soldiers and several million civilians died. The war destroyed four empires and led to the Russian Revolution and the Second World War.

events.title: The Armenian Genocide
events.summary: Beginning with the arrest of Armenian notables in Constantinople on 24 April 1915, the Ottoman government deports the Armenian population of Anatolia toward the Syrian desert in death marches and massacres. Around one million people — estimates range from 600,000 to 1.5 million — are killed, and an ancient homeland is emptied. It is the crime for which Raphael Lemkin later coins the word 'genocide', and its recognition remains contested by Turkey while commemorated by Armenians worldwide every 24 April.

events.title: The Russian Revolution
events.summary: Bread riots and mutinies in Petrograd toppled Tsar Nicholas II in March 1917; in November Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the provisional government and took Russia out of the war. A civil war that killed millions ended with the Soviet Union established in 1922, the first state to attempt to build a socialist society. Its planned industrialisation, famines and terror under Stalin, victory over Germany and rivalry with the United States shaped the twentieth century until its dissolution in 1991.

events.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
events.summary: An H1N1 influenza virus spread worldwide in three waves from early 1918, carried by troop movements at the end of the First World War. Estimates of the dead range from 17 to 50 million, possibly more, with India alone losing perhaps 12 million; unusually, young adults died in large numbers. Its origin is unknown; the name is an artefact of wartime censorship that spared neutral Spain's press. It remains the benchmark against which later pandemics are measured.

events.title: The March First Movement
events.summary: Thirty-three religious leaders read a declaration of independence in a Seoul restaurant, and within weeks perhaps two million Koreans had joined peaceful demonstrations in over a thousand places against Japanese rule. The colonial police and army killed thousands and arrested tens of thousands. The movement won no independence, but it produced a provisional government in Shanghai, forced Japan into a softer cultural policy, and is commemorated as a national holiday and named in the preamble of South Korea's constitution.

events.title: American women win the vote
events.summary: Seventy-two years after Seneca Falls, and after state-by-state campaigns, parades, hunger strikes and imprisonment, the Nineteenth Amendment barred the denial of the vote on account of sex; Tennessee ratified it by one vote in August 1920. It enfranchised some twenty-six million women at a stroke. It did not deliver the vote in practice to Black women in the South, who remained blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

events.title: The Ottoman Empire is dissolved
events.summary: Defeated in the First World War, occupied and partitioned, the Ottoman state ends when the Grand National Assembly under Mustafa Kemal abolishes the sultanate on 1 November 1922; the last sultan leaves Constantinople on a British warship. The Republic of Turkey is proclaimed the next year and the caliphate itself is abolished in 1924, closing an empire of six centuries whose former Arab provinces, drawn into new borders by Britain and France, still shape the region's politics.

events.title: Tutankhamun’s tomb is found intact
events.summary: On 26 November 1922 Howard Carter breaches a sealed doorway in the Valley of the Kings and, asked whether he can see anything, answers 'Yes, wonderful things'. The tomb of the minor pharaoh Tutankhamun, buried around 1323 BCE and protected by debris from later tomb-building, is the only royal burial of Egypt's New Kingdom found nearly intact — five thousand objects, including the solid-gold funerary mask that becomes ancient Egypt's global icon and transforms public fascination with archaeology.

events.title: Quantum mechanics is formulated
events.summary: Between 1925 and 1927 Werner Heisenberg's matrix mechanics, Erwin Schrödinger's wave equation, Paul Dirac's synthesis and Max Born's probabilistic interpretation produced a complete theory of the atomic world, built on Max Planck's quantum of 1900 and Niels Bohr's atom of 1913. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle set limits on what can be known. Quantum mechanics explains chemistry, semiconductors, lasers and nuclear physics, and its interpretation is still argued a century on.

events.title: Penicillin and the antibiotic age
events.summary: Alexander Fleming noticed in September 1928 that a mould contaminating a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital, London, had killed the surrounding bacteria, and named its active substance penicillin. It was Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley at Oxford who purified it and proved it cured infections in 1940–41, and American industry that mass-produced it by D-Day. Antibiotics have saved hundreds of millions of lives; resistance to them, which Fleming predicted, is now a global threat.

events.title: The Great Depression
events.summary: The Wall Street crash of October 1929 was followed by bank failures, collapsing trade and the deepest economic slump of the industrial era: US output fell by a quarter and unemployment reached a quarter of the workforce, with comparable distress in Germany, Latin America and beyond. Governments' responses ranged from Roosevelt's New Deal to the rise of the Nazis, who exploited German misery. The Depression discredited laissez-faire orthodoxy and produced Keynesian economics, welfare states and the institutions of Bretton Woods.

events.title: Gandhi's Salt March
events.summary: In March and April 1930 Mohandas Gandhi walked 390 kilometres from his ashram to the sea at Dandi and picked up a handful of salt, breaking the British monopoly and launching a nationwide campaign of civil disobedience in which some 60,000 people were jailed. It made satyagraha, non-violent resistance, the defining method of the Indian independence movement and a model for Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and others. India became independent in August 1947, partitioned from Pakistan amid mass violence.

events.title: The New Deal remakes the American state
events.summary: With a quarter of the workforce unemployed, Roosevelt's administration put banks under federal guarantee, hired millions through the Civilian Conservation Corps and the WPA to build roads, schools, dams and murals, gave unions a protected right to organise, and in 1935 created Social Security — old-age pensions and unemployment insurance. Farm and domestic workers, disproportionately Black, were excluded from much of it. Recovery was incomplete until the war, but the idea that the federal government is answerable for the economy dates from here.

events.title: Haile Selassie appeals to the League of Nations
events.summary: Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 with aircraft and mustard gas, and in June 1936 the exiled emperor stood before the League of Nations in Geneva to ask what collective security was worth. Italian journalists heckled him; the League's sanctions were lifted within weeks. His warning that small states would be next was quoted everywhere after 1939. Ethiopia was liberated in 1941, and the speech made Haile Selassie a symbol for anti-colonial movements far beyond Africa.
